questions.stem: Which statement best describes the default behaviour of Cilium's eBPF NodePort implementation with respect to SNAT?

options.text: It operates in SNAT mode by default, redirecting requests to remote backends on the node's behalf and requiring replies to make an extra hop back for reverse SNAT translation.
It operates in DSR mode by default, with backends replying directly to external clients using the service IP/port as source.
It operates in a hybrid mode by default, using DSR for TCP and SNAT for UDP.
It operates without any address translation by default, relying on the client to route replies.

questions.explanation: By default the eBPF NodePort implementation operates in SNAT mode: the node redirects the request to the remote backend on its behalf by performing SNAT, and replies from the backend make the extra hop back to that node for reverse SNAT translation.

optionRationale.b: DSR mode is not the default; it is enabled by changing loadBalancer.mode to dsr.
optionRationale.c: The hybrid mode is described as an optimisation available with DSR, not as the default.
optionRationale.d: The default explicitly performs SNAT, so it is not translation-free.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR)
citations.quote: By default, Cilium's eBPF NodePort implementation operates in SNAT mode.

questions.stem: A cluster's Kubernetes control plane cannot be configured to allocate PodCIDRs to nodes, so the platform team enables Cilium's cluster-pool IPAM mode instead. What does each Cilium agent do on startup in this mode?

options.text: It waits until the podCIDRs range is made available via the Cilium Node object for all enabled address families.
It allocates PodCIDRs itself from the cluster CIDR and writes them back to the Kubernetes Node object.
It starts immediately and requests individual pod IPs from the Hubble Relay on demand.
It falls back to the Kubernetes host-scope allocator until a PodCIDR is assigned.

questions.explanation: In cluster-pool IPAM mode the agent does not begin allocating until the podCIDRs range has been published for every enabled address family through the Cilium Node object. This mode exists precisely for clusters where Kubernetes cannot hand out PodCIDRs or where finer control is required.

optionRationale.b: The agent waits for the range to be provided; it does not derive PodCIDRs from the cluster CIDR and write them to the Kubernetes Node object.
optionRationale.c: The agent waits for a PodCIDR range rather than starting immediately, and pod IP allocation is not performed by Hubble Relay.
optionRationale.d: No fallback to the Kubernetes host-scope allocator is described; the agent waits for the range instead.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
In this mode, the Cilium agent will wait on startup until the ``podCIDRs`` range
are made available via the Cilium Node ``v2.CiliumNode`` object for all enabled
address families

questions.stem: A Cilium operator is creating an ENI. `spec.eni.security-groups` is not set, but `spec.eni.security-group-tags` is set. How are the Security Group IDs for the new ENI determined?

options.text: The operator lists all Security Groups in the account and attaches the ones that match the list of tags.
The new ENI inherits the security group IDs of `eth0` of the instance.
The operator attaches every Security Group in the account.
The operator attaches the Security Groups whose IDs are listed in `spec.eni.security-groups`.

questions.explanation: With `spec.eni.security-groups` unset and `spec.eni.security-group-tags` set, the operator lists all Security Groups in the account and attaches those matching the tags.

optionRationale.b: Inheriting from `eth0` is the final fallback, used only when neither `security-groups` nor `security-group-tags` is set.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says the operator attaches the ones that match the tags, not all Security Groups.
optionRationale.d: `spec.eni.security-groups` is not set in this scenario, so its IDs cannot be used.

citations.title: ENI Creation
citations.quote:
the operator will list all Security Groups in the account and will attach to
the ENI the ones that match the list of tags passed.

questions.stem: An engineer sets `monitor-aggregation` to `low` and enables socket load-balancing. Which description matches the resulting tracing behaviour?

options.text: A tracing event is generated on every send packet, and reverse-direction (recv) socket trace events are suppressed.
A tracing event is generated on every receive and send packet, and all socket trace events are emitted.
A tracing event is generated only for connect system calls, and no packet events are produced.
A tracing event is generated on every new connection and on average once per interval, and all socket trace events are emitted.

questions.explanation: At the `low` level a tracing event is generated on every send packet. When socket load-balancing is enabled, the `lowest`/`low` level suppresses reverse-direction (recv) socket trace events.

optionRationale.b: That combines the `none` packet behaviour with the `none` socket behaviour, not `low`.
optionRationale.c: Emitting socket trace events only for connect system calls corresponds to `medium`/`maximum`, not `low`.
optionRationale.d: The new-connection and interval behaviour belongs to `medium`, and emitting all socket trace events belongs to `none`.

citations.title: ConfigMap Options
citations.quote: ``low`` - Generate a tracing event on every send packet.

questions.stem: An engineer runs Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement with socket-LB enabled. A pod has an established connected UDP socket to a Service backend, and that backend is then deleted. What does the Cilium agent do?

options.text: It forcefully terminates the application socket connected to the deleted backend so the application can be load-balanced to active backends.
It leaves the socket untouched and silently drops all further packets from that socket until the application closes it.
It rewrites the socket's destination to the Service cluster IP and keeps the connection alive indefinitely.
It disables socket-LB for that pod and falls back to iptables masquerading for the remainder of the connection.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that when socket-LB is enabled, pods can keep sending traffic to a deleted backend, and Cilium handles this by forcefully terminating application sockets connected to deleted backends so applications can be load-balanced to active backends.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says Cilium forcefully terminates such sockets, not that it leaves them and drops packets.
optionRationale.c: No such rewriting of the destination to the cluster IP is described; the described action is termination of the socket.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not describe disabling socket-LB or falling back to iptables in this situation.

citations.title: Limitations
citations.quote:
Cilium agent
      handles such scenarios by forcefully terminating application sockets that are connected
      to deleted backends, so that the applications can be load-balanced to active backends.

questions.stem: A pod is scheduled onto a node in a Cilium cluster. Which component is invoked by Kubernetes at that moment to trigger the datapath configuration that gives the pod networking, load-balancing and network policies?

options.text: The Cilium Operator, because it handles duties that must be performed once for the entire cluster.
The CNI plugin (`cilium-cni`), which interacts with the Cilium API of the node.
The debug CLI client (`cilium-dbg`), which accesses the eBPF maps directly.
The `cilium` command line tool, using `kubeconfig` information to reach the cluster.

questions.explanation: The CNI plugin is the component Kubernetes invokes when a pod is scheduled or terminated on a node; it then talks to the node's Cilium API to trigger the datapath configuration for that pod. The operator handles cluster-wide duties, the debug CLI inspects the local agent, and the `cilium` CLI is for installing, managing and troubleshooting from outside the cluster.

optionRationale.a: The operator is described as handling duties logically handled once for the entire cluster, not as the component invoked per pod by Kubernetes.
optionRationale.c: ``cilium-dbg`` is for inspecting the state and status of the local agent and accessing eBPF maps, not for triggering pod datapath configuration.
optionRationale.d: The ``cilium`` CLI is typically installed remote from the cluster and is used for quick-installing, managing and troubleshooting, not invoked by Kubernetes on pod scheduling.

citations.title: Cilium
citations.quote:
The CNI plugin (``cilium-cni``) is invoked by Kubernetes when a pod is
  scheduled or terminated on a node.

questions.stem: An engineer installs Cilium with Helm using `--set ipam.mode=kubernetes` and `--set k8s.requireIPv4PodCIDR=true`. What is the effect of the second setting?

options.text: The Cilium agent waits until an IPv4 PodCIDR is made available via the Kubernetes node resource.
The Cilium agent allocates IPv4 pod addresses from a cluster-wide pool held in the Cilium operator.
The Cilium agent refuses to start unless the Kubernetes node already has an IPv6 PodCIDR assigned.
The Cilium agent advertises the node's IPv4 PodCIDR to other nodes using BGP.

questions.explanation: The `k8s-require-ipv4-pod-cidr` option instructs the Cilium agent to wait until an IPv4 PodCIDR is made available via the Kubernetes node resource. The Helm equivalent is `--set k8s.requireIPv4PodCIDR=true`, which only works together with `--set ipam.mode=kubernetes`.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes waiting for a PodCIDR on the node resource, not allocating from a cluster-wide pool in the operator.
optionRationale.c: The option concerns the IPv4 PodCIDR, not the IPv6 one, and it makes the agent wait rather than refuse to start.
optionRationale.d: BGP advertisement of PodCIDRs is not mentioned; the option only governs waiting for the PodCIDR to appear.

citations.title: Configuration
citations.quote:
instructs the Cilium agent to wait until
   an IPv4 PodCIDR is made available via the Kubernetes node resource.

questions.stem: An engineer sets `monitor-aggregation` to `maximum` in the Cilium ConfigMap and expects the most aggressive coalescing available. What tracing behaviour results?

options.text: It is equivalent to `medium`, so events are generated for send packets on every new connection, on unseen TCP flags, and on average once per interval.
It generates a tracing event on every receive and send packet.
It generates a tracing event on every send packet only.
It suppresses all tracing events except packets dropped by Cilium.

questions.explanation: `maximum` is described as an alias for the most aggressive aggregation level, and currently it is equivalent to setting `monitor-aggregation` to `medium`. The `medium` behaviour is the one described for new connections, unseen TCP flags and the reporting interval.

optionRationale.b: That is the behaviour of `none`, which generates an event on every receive and send packet.
optionRationale.c: That is the behaviour of `low`, which generates an event on every send packet.
optionRationale.d: Dropped packets do produce one event per packet at `medium`, but `maximum` is not a drop-only mode; it is equivalent to `medium`.

citations.title: ConfigMap Options
citations.quote:
``maximum`` - An alias for the most aggressive aggregation level. Currently
    this is equivalent to setting ``monitor-aggregation`` to ``medium``.

questions.stem: A LoadBalancer service has spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges set to 192.168.1.0/24. By default, which services does this CIDR restriction apply to?

options.text: Only the LoadBalancer service, not the corresponding NodePort or ClusterIP services.
The LoadBalancer service and its corresponding NodePort service, but not ClusterIP.
All service types created for the service, including NodePort and ClusterIP.
Only the ClusterIP service, because NodePort and LoadBalancer are externally exposed.

questions.explanation: By default the white-listed CIDRs in spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges apply only to the LoadBalancer service, not to the NodePort or ClusterIP services that are installed alongside it.

optionRationale.b: The restriction does not extend to NodePort by default.
optionRationale.c: Propagating to all externally exposed types requires the Helm option bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true.
optionRationale.d: The restriction applies to the LoadBalancer service, not the ClusterIP service.

citations.title: LoadBalancer Source Ranges Checks
citations.quote: By default the specified white-listed CIDRs in ``spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges`` only apply to the ``LoadBalancer`` service, but not the corresponding ``NodePort`` or ``ClusterIP`` service which get installed along with the ``LoadBalancer`` service.

options.text: Due to not depending on any underlying networking limitations, the available addressing space is potentially much larger and allows to run any number of pods per node if the PodCIDR size is configured accordingly.

Cilium will assign IPs to pods out of the PodCIDR assigned to the specific Kubernetes node. By using `Alias IP ranges <https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/alias-ip>`_, these IPs are natively routable on Google Cloud's network without additional encapsulation or route distribution.
All traffic not staying with the ``ipv4-native-routing-cidr`` will be masqueraded to the node's IP address to become publicly routable.

The default choice to store any data and propagate state is to use Kubernetes custom resource definitions (CRDs). CRDs are offered by Kubernetes for cluster components to represent configurations and state via Kubernetes resources.

questions.explanation: The default choice to store any data and propagate state is to use Kubernetes custom resource definitions (CRDs). CRDs are offered by Kubernetes for cluster components to represent configurations and state via Kubernetes resources.

optionRationale.a: This describes Addressing space, not Kubernetes CRDs.
optionRationale.b: This describes Addressing, not Kubernetes CRDs.
optionRationale.c: This describes Masquerading, not Kubernetes CRDs.

citations.quote: The default choice to store any data and propagate state is to use Kubernetes custom resource definitions (CRDs). CRDs are offered by Kubernetes for cluster components to represent configurations and state via Kubernetes resources.

questions.stem: A Cilium cluster uses DSR with IPIP and also selective service node exposure via the service.cilium.io/node annotation. The service is exposed only on nodes labeled service.cilium.io/node=beefy. Where must the backend Pods run?

options.text: On any node in the cluster, because the load balancing node fully translates the traffic.
On nodes that are part of the exposure set (nodes labeled service.cilium.io/node=beefy).
On nodes that are not part of the exposure set, to avoid conflicts.
On the same node as the load balancer frontend, regardless of labels.

questions.explanation: With DSR IPIP combined with selective service node exposure, the backend Pods must run on nodes that are part of the exposure set because the backend node terminates the inbound IPIP traffic and rewrites the reply, requiring the service to be present on the backend node. Only nodes that host neither the frontend nor any backend may be left out. The other options are incorrect: SNAT forwarding allows backends anywhere, but DSR IPIP does not; nodes outside the exposure set cannot host backends; and co-location with the frontend is not required.

optionRationale.a: This describes SNAT forwarding, not DSR IPIP.
optionRationale.c: Backends must be on nodes in the exposure set, not outside it.
optionRationale.d: There is no requirement for backends to be on the same node as the frontend; they must be on nodes in the exposure set.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR) with IPIP
citations.quote:
Therefore, when DSR
    IPIP is combined with `Selective Service Node Exposure`_, the backend Pods
    must run on nodes that are part of the exposure set

questions.stem: An engineer wants to prevent Cilium from creating the NodePort and ClusterIP services that normally accompany a LoadBalancer service. Which annotation achieves this?

options.text: service.cilium.io/type: LoadBalancer
service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy: deny
service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy: allow
bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true

questions.explanation: The service.cilium.io/type annotation set to LoadBalancer avoids the creation of corresponding NodePort and ClusterIP services.

optionRationale.b: src-ranges-policy: deny turns the CIDR list into a deny-list; it does not affect service creation.
optionRationale.c: src-ranges-policy: allow is the default allow-list behaviour; it does not affect service creation.
optionRationale.d: bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes is a Helm value that propagates CIDRs to other service types; it does not prevent their creation.

questions.stem: An engineer is migrating a kind cluster from cluster-pool to multi-pool IPAM mode. They execute a Helm upgrade command that includes the flag `--set-string extraConfig.enable-cluster-pool-to-multi-pool-migration=true` and `--set operator.rollOutPods=true`. What is the immediate operational effect of this specific combination of flags on the Cilium components?

options.text: It updates the Cilium ConfigMap and restarts only the Cilium operator, allowing it to create the default CiliumPodIPPool.
It restarts all Cilium agents immediately, forcing them to switch to multi-pool mode before the operator creates the pool.
It deletes all existing CiliumNode resources and recreates them with the new multi-pool IPAM configuration.
It pauses the Cilium operator and prevents any new Pod IP allocations until the migration is manually verified.

questions.explanation: The source states that the command 'updates the Cilium ConfigMap and restarts only the Cilium operator'. It explicitly sets `rollOutCiliumPods=false` in the example, meaning agents are not restarted by this initial command. The operator is responsible for creating the default pool.

optionRationale.b: Incorrect because the example sets `rollOutCiliumPods=false`, so agents are not restarted by the initial Helm upgrade. Agents are restarted manually later in the process.
optionRationale.c: Incorrect because the migration preserves existing per-node CIDRs and does not delete CiliumNode resources; it updates their `spec.ipam` fields.
optionRationale.d: Incorrect because the source does not mention pausing the operator or preventing allocations; it describes a rolling migration where connectivity is maintained.

citations.title: Practical Example
citations.quote: The command updates the Cilium ConfigMap and restarts only the Cilium operator

questions.stem: An existing cluster is running kube-proxy as a DaemonSet. An engineer wants to remove kube-proxy to prepare for Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement. Which sequence of commands should they use?

options.text: kubectl -n kube-system delete ds kube-proxy; kubectl -n kube-system delete cm kube-proxy; iptables-save | grep -v KUBE | iptables-restore
kubectl -n kube-system delete ds kube-proxy; kubectl -n kube-system delete cm kube-proxy; iptables-save | grep KUBE | iptables-restore
kubectl -n kube-system delete ds kube-proxy; kubectl -n kube-system delete cm kube-proxy; iptables -F
kubectl -n kube-system delete ds kube-proxy; kubectl -n kube-system delete cm kube-proxy; systemctl restart kubelet

questions.explanation: The excerpt provides the exact commands: delete the kube-proxy DaemonSet, delete the kube-proxy ConfigMap to avoid reinstallation during a kubeadm upgrade, and run on each node with root permissions: iptables-save | grep -v KUBE | iptables-restore. This removes KUBE-related iptables rules.

optionRationale.b: The grep pattern is inverted; it would keep only KUBE rules instead of removing them.
optionRationale.c: iptables -F flushes all rules, which is not what the excerpt recommends.
optionRationale.d: Restarting kubelet is not mentioned in the excerpt for this purpose.

citations.title: Quick-Start
citations.quote:
$ kubectl -n kube-system delete ds kube-proxy
$ # Delete the configmap as well to avoid kube-proxy being reinstalled during a Kubeadm upgrade
$ kubectl -n kube-system delete cm kube-proxy
$ # Run on each node with root permissions:
$ iptables-save | grep -v KUBE | iptables-restore

questions.stem: A cluster runs Cilium in CRD-backed IPAM mode. An operator removes an address from spec.ipam.available on a CiliumNode while that address is still allocated to a running pod. What is the result?

options.text: The pod keeps the address, and the address will not be available for re-allocation after it is released.
The pod is immediately restarted and receives a new address from the remaining pool.
The address is returned to the pool at once and can be handed to another pod.
The Cilium agent rejects the update and restores the address in spec.ipam.available.

questions.explanation: Removing an address that is currently allocated does not disrupt the pod using it: the address continues to be used, but once released it is not offered for re-allocation.

optionRationale.b: Nothing in the mode triggers a restart of pods when the pool shrinks; the allocated address simply stays in use.
optionRationale.c: The address is explicitly not made available for re-allocation after release, so it cannot be handed out again.
optionRationale.d: The agent updates its pool from the field; it does not reject the change or write the address back.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote: When an IP is removed that is currently allocated, the IP will continue to be used but will not be available for re-allocation after release.

questions.stem: An engineer wants Cilium's native `hostPort` support in a cluster and is considering setting the Helm CNI chaining option `cni.chainingMode=portmap`. What does Cilium require instead?

options.text: Setting `kubeProxyReplacement=true`, which automatically enables native hostPort support with no further action required.
Setting `cni.chainingMode=portmap` together with `kubeProxyReplacement=true`, since both are needed for host port mapping.
Creating a Kubernetes Service of type NodePort for each host port, because host port is configured through a service object.
Nothing at all: host port support is part of kube-proxy and is inherited automatically by Cilium.

questions.explanation: Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement natively supports `hostPort` service mapping without the Helm CNI chaining option `cni.chainingMode=portmap`. Specifying `kubeProxyReplacement=true` enables the native hostPort support automatically, so no further action is required.

optionRationale.b: The portmap chaining mode is explicitly not needed for native hostPort support, so combining it with `kubeProxyReplacement=true` is not the requirement.
optionRationale.c: Host port is not configured through a Kubernetes service object; it piggy-backs on user-configured defaults of the service handling behaviour.
optionRationale.d: Host port support is described as not part of kube-proxy; it comes from Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement.

citations.title: Container HostPort Support
citations.quote:
Although not part of kube-proxy, Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement also
natively supports ``hostPort`` service mapping without having to use the
Helm CNI chaining option of ``cni.chainingMode=portmap``.

optionRationale.c: `AllocateAddress` is not mentioned; the create call is `CreateNetworkInterface`.

questions.stem: Which Helm values are required to enable per-service DSR with IPIP dispatch using the service.cilium.io/forwarding-mode: dsr annotation?

options.text: bpf.lbModeAnnotation=true and loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip
loadBalancer.mode=dsr and bpf.lbAlgorithmAnnotation=true
bpf.lbModeAnnotation=true and loadBalancer.mode=snat
loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=geneve and bpf.lbModeAnnotation=true

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that annotation-based DSR requires bpf.lbModeAnnotation=true together with an explicit loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip to define how per-service DSR packets are dispatched. The other options are incorrect: loadBalancer.mode=dsr is not mentioned as required (the example keeps the global default as SNAT), loadBalancer.mode=snat alone is not sufficient, and geneve is a different dispatch mode.

optionRationale.b: loadBalancer.mode=dsr is not required; the example keeps loadBalancer.mode=snat.
optionRationale.c: loadBalancer.mode=snat is the global default but does not enable DSR IPIP by itself.
optionRationale.d: geneve is a different dispatch mode, not IPIP.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR) with IPIP
citations.quote:
this requires
``bpf.lbModeAnnotation=true`` together with an explicit
``loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip`` to define how the per-service DSR packets are
dispatched to backends.

questions.stem: A platform team wants to rate limit individual Pods using Cilium's bandwidth manager. A colleague suggests deploying the Kubernetes bandwidth CNI plugin alongside Cilium, arguing that Cilium will chain to it. Which statement best describes how Cilium's bandwidth manager relates to that plugin?

options.text: Cilium's bandwidth manager is natively integrated into Cilium, does not rely on CNI chaining, and does not make use of the bandwidth CNI plugin.
Cilium's bandwidth manager requires the bandwidth CNI plugin to be installed first, because it delegates all shaping to that plugin.
Cilium's bandwidth manager chains to the bandwidth CNI plugin only when tunnelling mode is enabled.
Cilium's bandwidth manager replaces the bandwidth CNI plugin's TBF implementation with a second CNI plugin that Cilium invokes at Pod creation.

questions.explanation: The bandwidth manager is described as natively integrated into Cilium and explicitly does not rely on CNI chaining, so it does not use the bandwidth CNI plugin at all. The plugin is in fact discouraged because of scalability concerns, particularly for multi-queue network interfaces, since it is based on TBF rather than EDT.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt states the opposite: the bandwidth manager does not rely on CNI chaining and does not make use of the bandwidth CNI plugin.
optionRationale.c: No such conditional chaining is described; the bandwidth manager is natively integrated and does not use the plugin in any mode.
optionRationale.d: Cilium does not invoke a second CNI plugin; the bandwidth manager is natively integrated into Cilium itself.

The bandwidth manager does not rely on CNI chaining and is natively integrated
into Cilium instead. Hence, it does not make use of the `bandwidth CNI

questions.stem: A cluster's kube-apiserver has been configured to use the NodePort range 10000-32767 instead of the Kubernetes default. What must be done on the Cilium side?

options.text: Pass the same range to Cilium via nodePort.range, for example nodePort.range="10000\,32767".
Nothing; Cilium always assumes the default range of 30000-32767.
Set nodePort.autoProtectPortRanges to false so the new range is accepted.
Set nodePort.bindProtection to false so the new range is accepted.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that if kube-apiserver was configured to use a non-default NodePort port range, then the same range must be passed to Cilium via the nodePort.range option, giving nodePort.range="10000\,32767" for a range of 10000-32767.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt gives 30000-32767 only as the default Kubernetes NodePort range; it explicitly requires passing a non-default range to Cilium.
optionRationale.c: autoProtectPortRanges controls whether the NodePort range is appended to the reserved ports, not whether a non-default range is communicated to Cilium.
optionRationale.d: bindProtection controls whether application bind(2) requests to NodePort service ports are prevented, not the port range configuration.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Key-Value Store in Cilium?

options.text: When running together with an orchestration system such as Kubernetes, the list of all nodes in the cluster including their associated allocation prefix node is made available to each agent automatically. New nodes joining the cluster will automatically be incorporated into the mesh.

Due to not depending on any underlying networking limitations, the available addressing space is potentially much larger and allows to run any number of pods per node if the PodCIDR size is configured accordingly.

The Cilium debug CLI client (``cilium-dbg``) is a command-line tool that is installed along with the Cilium agent. It interacts with the REST API of the Cilium agent running on the same node. The debug CLI allows inspecting the state and status of the local agent. It also provides tooling to directly access the eBPF maps to validate their state.

All requirements for state storage and propagation can be met with Kubernetes CRDs as configured in the default configuration of Cilium. A key-value store can optionally be used as an optimization to improve the scalability of a cluster as change notifications and storage requirements are more efficient with direct key-value store usage.

questions.explanation: All requirements for state storage and propagation can be met with Kubernetes CRDs as configured in the default configuration of Cilium. A key-value store can optionally be used as an optimization to improve the scalability of a cluster as change notifications and storage requirements are more efficient with direct key-value store usage.

optionRationale.a: This describes Auto-configuration, not Key-Value Store.
optionRationale.c: This describes Debug Client, not Key-Value Store.
optionRationale.b: This describes Addressing space, not Key-Value Store.

questions.stem: On an Azure cluster, the Cilium operator has just discovered existing interfaces with associated IPs on an instance. Where does it publish those addresses so that the agent on the node can use them?

options.text: In the spec.ipam.available field of the node's CiliumNode resource
In the status.ipam.used field of the node's CiliumNode resource
In the .Spec.ProviderID field of the Kubernetes Node resource
In the agent configuration option for Azure allocation parameters

questions.explanation: The operator scans Azure instances for existing interfaces with associated IPs and makes them available through spec.ipam.available. The status.ipam.used field is where it monitors addresses already in use, not where it publishes newly discovered ones.

optionRationale.b: status.ipam.used is monitored by the operator to track addresses in use; discovered addresses are published in spec.ipam.available.
optionRationale.c: .Spec.ProviderID is read by the agent to derive the Azure instance ID; it does not carry IP addresses.
optionRationale.d: Azure allocation parameters are agent configuration passed into the custom resource; they are not the field holding discovered IPs.

It scans the Azure instances

questions.stem: A pod on node A sends traffic to a pod on node B, and no network security policies exist in the cluster. What is the result?

options.text: The traffic is dropped until a policy explicitly allows it.
The traffic is allowed, because in the absence of any network security policies all Pods can reach each other.
The traffic is allowed only if both pods share the same identity.
The traffic is masqueraded as it leaves node A, because the destination pod is outside the cluster.

questions.explanation: Cilium does not block pod-to-pod traffic by default. Only once network security policies are in place does reachability become restricted, so with no policies at all every pod can reach every other pod.

optionRationale.a: This describes default-deny, which applies only once policies are in place; the excerpt states the opposite for the no-policy case.
optionRationale.c: Identity is not a precondition for connectivity here; the excerpt says all Pods can reach each other in the absence of policies.
optionRationale.d: Masquerading applies to traffic leaving the cluster as a client, not to pod-to-pod traffic between nodes.

citations.title: Pod-to-Pod Connectivity
citations.quote:
In the absence of any
network security policies, all Pods can reach each other.

questions.stem: A team wants the CIDR list in loadBalancerSourceRanges to block traffic from certain CIDRs while allowing everything else. Which annotation and value achieve this?

options.text: service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy: deny
service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy: allow
service.cilium.io/type: LoadBalancer
bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true

questions.explanation: Cilium supports turning the list into a deny-list through the service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy annotation, which accepts allow or deny; setting it to deny blocks traffic from the listed CIDRs while allowing the rest.

optionRationale.b: The allow value is the default behaviour, which treats the list as an allow-list rather than a deny-list.
optionRationale.c: The service.cilium.io/type annotation is used to avoid creating corresponding NodePort and ClusterIP services, not to invert the CIDR policy.
optionRationale.d: bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes is a Helm option that propagates the CIDRs to all externally exposed service types; it does not turn the list into a deny-list.

citations.title: LoadBalancer Source Ranges Checks
citations.quote:
This
behavior can be achieved through the ``service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy``
annotation which accepts the values of ``allow`` or ``deny``.

questions.stem: Why is it not possible to directly delete or update the CIDRs already in use within an existing CiliumPodIPPool resource?

options.text: To prevent pods from receiving IPs from a new range while some pods still use the old IP pool on the same nodes.
Because the Cilium operator does not support modifying the spec.ipv4.cidrs field of an existing resource.
To ensure that all nodes in the cluster are updated simultaneously to avoid network partitioning.
Because the Kubernetes API server rejects any changes to the CIDR maskSize of an active pool.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explicitly states: "This restriction prevents pods from receiving IPs from a new range while some pods still use the old IP pool on the same nodes."

optionRationale.b: Incorrect because the excerpt shows that the CIDR can be updated, but it requires a specific migration process involving node groups.
optionRationale.c: Incorrect because the process involves splitting the cluster into two node groups, not updating all nodes simultaneously.
optionRationale.d: Incorrect because the restriction is about the CIDR range itself, not specifically the maskSize, and the API does allow the update as part of the migration steps.

It must match the containerPort value exactly.
It must be chosen from the range reserved for the loopback address.

questions.explanation: The hostPort must not fall inside the configured NodePort port range, so that collisions are avoided.

optionRationale.a: No privileged-port restriction is stated; the stated constraint concerns the NodePort range.
optionRationale.c: The example maps containerPort 80 to hostPort 8080, so the two need not match.
optionRationale.d: No such reserved range is described; loopback is mentioned only as an access path.

questions.stem: An engineer wants to confirm from the command line whether the HostPort feature has been enabled in Cilium. Which command and indicator should be used?

iptables-save, checking for a HOSTPORT rule in the host namespace.
kubectl get nodes -o wide, checking that each node has an INTERNAL-IP.
cilium-dbg service list, checking that a NodePort service type is present.

questions.explanation: The cilium-dbg status CLI command provides visibility through the KubeProxyReplacement info line, and when the feature is enabled successfully HostPort is shown as Enabled.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt shows that no iptables rule for the HostPort service is present, so this is not the verification method.
optionRationale.c: Node IP visibility is a prerequisite for exposure, not a check that the HostPort feature is enabled.
optionRationale.d: The service list shows HostPort entries, but the stated verification of enablement is the status info line.

questions.stem: A single EndpointSlice contains two endpoints, `10.0.0.11` and `10.0.0.12`, and is annotated with `service.cilium.io/weight: "70"`. How does the weight apply?

options.text: It applies only to the first endpoint in the slice.
It applies to all backends in that EndpointSlice.
It is divided evenly between the two endpoints.
It applies only to endpoints that also carry the annotation.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the configured weight applies to all backends in a given EndpointSlice.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says the weight applies to all backends, not just the first.
optionRationale.c: No division between endpoints is described.
optionRationale.d: The annotation is on the EndpointSlice, not on individual endpoints.

questions.stem: An engineer wants pods in namespace `empire` to draw IPv4 addresses from one pool and IPv6 addresses from a different pool, without relying on label selectors. Which annotations should be set?

options.text: ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool for both families, applied twice
ipam.cilium.io/ipv4-pool=<pool-name> and ipam.cilium.io/ipv6-pool=<pool-name>
ipam.cilium.io/require-pool-match="true" together with ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool
spec.podSelector and spec.namespaceSelector on the CiliumPodIPPool

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that different pools can be specified for IPv4 and IPv6 using the ipv4-pool and ipv6-pool annotations. These can be placed on the pod or on its namespace.

optionRationale.a: The plain ip-pool annotation names a single pool; the per-family variants exist precisely to name different pools for each family.
optionRationale.c: require-pool-match only blocks allocation until a non-default pool matches; it does not select per-family pools.
optionRationale.d: Selectors are the second precedence step, not the way to name different pools per IP family.

citations.quote:
You can specify different pools for IPv4 and IPv6 using the

questions.stem: A cluster runs in `multi-pool` IPAM mode with a single `CiliumPodIPPool` named `default` whose IPv4 CIDR is `10.10.0.0/16`. An engineer applies a change that replaces that CIDR with `10.20.0.0/16` while pods on two nodes still hold addresses from the old range. What does the Cilium operator do in response?

options.text: It logs a warning for each CIDR block still in use by a node but removed from the pool.
It refuses the update and reverts the pool to the previous CIDR.
It silently reassigns the affected pods to addresses from the new CIDR.
It deletes the `CiliumNodes` of the affected nodes automatically.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the operator reports a warning for each CIDR block still in use by a node but removed from the pool, and shows the corresponding log lines with `msg="CIDR from pool still in use by node"`. The update itself is accepted; the operator does not revert it, reassign pod IPs, or delete `CiliumNodes` on its own — those are manual steps in the migration procedure.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt shows the update being applied and the operator merely warning; nothing reverts the pool.
optionRationale.c: Reassigning IPs is done by evicting and rescheduling workloads, not by the operator silently.
optionRationale.d: Deleting `CiliumNodes` is a manual step performed with `kubectl delete cn` for each node group.

A CiliumNetworkPolicy in the agent's own namespace
The CiliumNodeConfig resource for the local node
The PodCIDR field of the Kubernetes Node object

optionRationale.c: The excerpt names only ciliumnodes.cilium.io as the resource the agent watches.

questions.stem: A CiliumNode has `spec.eni.security-groups` populated with a list of Security Group IDs, and `spec.eni.security-group-tags` is also populated. Which Security Groups are attached to the newly created ENI?

options.text: The IDs listed in `spec.eni.security-groups`.
The Security Groups in the account matching `spec.eni.security-group-tags`.
The Security Group IDs of `eth0` of the instance.
The union of the IDs in `spec.eni.security-groups` and the tag-matched Security Groups.

questions.explanation: The excerpt gives a strict order: `spec.eni.security-groups` is consulted first, and if set those are the IDs attached, so the tag field is never reached.

optionRationale.b: Tag matching is only consulted when `spec.eni.security-groups` is not set.
optionRationale.c: Inheriting from `eth0` is the last resort, used only when neither of the other fields is set.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes a precedence order, not a union of the two sources.

citations.quote:

questions.stem: You are configuring the network adapter on an `m5n.xlarge` node so that Cilium's XDP acceleration can be deployed. Running `ethtool -l eth0` shows `Combined: 4` under the current hardware settings. Which command sets the channels to a value permitted for XDP?

options.text: `sudo ethtool -L eth0 combined 2`
`sudo ethtool -L eth0 combined 4`
`sudo ethtool -L eth0 combined 3`
`sudo ip link set dev eth0 mtu 3498`

questions.explanation: The excerpt says that in order to use XDP the channels must be set to at most 1/2 of the value from `Combined`, and shows the command `sudo ethtool -L eth0 combined 2` for the `m5n.xlarge` instance whose default `Combined` is 4. Half of 4 is 2, so setting combined to 2 is permitted.

optionRationale.b: Leaving combined at 4 does not satisfy the requirement that channels be at most 1/2 of the `Combined` value.
optionRationale.c: 3 is more than half of 4, so it exceeds the maximum permitted for XDP.
optionRationale.d: This command changes the MTU, not the channel count; the excerpt applies MTU and channel changes as separate commands.

citations.title: NodePort XDP on AWS
citations.quote:
In order to use XDP the channels must be set to at most 1/2 of the value from
``Combined`` above.

The Hubble CLI (``hubble``) is a command-line tool able to connect to either the gRPC API of ``hubble-relay`` or the local server to retrieve flow events.
Only honored for the Service referenced by that ``EndpointSlice`` when it uses the Maglev load-balancing algorithm, whether Maglev is configured globally or selected per service through ``service.
All traffic not staying with the ``ipv4-native-routing-cidr`` will be masqueraded to the node's IP address to become publicly routable.

optionRationale.a: This describes Graphical UI, not Masquerading.
optionRationale.c: This describes Weights, not Masquerading.

questions.stem: A team is triaging an incident and wants to know how many 5xx and 4xx HTTP response codes a particular service is returning, and also wants the same figure across all clusters. Which pair of questions does Cilium's observability layer address?

options.text: The rate of 5xx or 4xx HTTP response codes for a particular service, and the same rate across all clusters.
The rate of TCP retransmissions for a particular service, and the same rate across all clusters.
The rate of DNS NXDOMAIN responses for a particular service, and the same rate across all clusters.
The rate of dropped packets for a particular service, and the same rate across all clusters.

questions.explanation: The excerpt opens with the question of the rate of 5xx or 4xx HTTP response codes for a particular service or across all clusters. The other options substitute different metrics that the excerpt does not mention.

optionRationale.b: TCP retransmission rates are not among the questions listed in the excerpt.
optionRationale.c: DNS NXDOMAIN response rates are not among the questions listed in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: Dropped packet rates are not among the questions listed in the excerpt.

questions.stem: An engineer notices that the Cilium operator keeps allocating additional IP addresses on an Azure node even though pods are not currently being created there. What explains this behaviour?

options.text: The operator allocates more IPs as needed to meet the IP pre-allocation watermark, so that IPs are always available
The operator allocates one IP per CiliumNode resource created on the node, regardless of demand
The agent requests a new IP each time it reads the .Spec.ProviderID field of the Node resource
The operator re-allocates every address listed in status.ipam.used on each reconciliation loop

questions.explanation: The operator constantly monitors used addresses in status.ipam.used and allocates more IPs as needed to meet the IP pre-allocation watermark, which is what keeps a pool of addresses ready ahead of demand.

optionRationale.b: The number of CiliumNode resources is not what drives allocation; the pre-allocation watermark does.
optionRationale.c: Reading .Spec.ProviderID is how the agent derives the Azure instance ID at startup, not a trigger for IP allocation.
optionRationale.d: status.ipam.used is monitored to see which addresses are in use; the operator does not re-allocate them each loop.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
It will then constantly monitor the used IP
addresses in the ``status.ipam.used`` field and allocate more IPs as needed to
meet the IP pre-allocation watermark.

questions.stem: A Cilium operator is creating an ENI. Neither `spec.eni.security-groups` nor `spec.eni.security-group-tags` is set. Which Security Group IDs are attached to the new ENI?

options.text: The security group IDs of `eth0` of the instance.
The security group IDs of the primary ENI of the instance.
No Security Group IDs are attached.
The security group IDs of every ENI on the instance.

questions.explanation: When neither field is set, the newly created ENI inherits the security group IDs of `eth0` of the instance.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt names `eth0` specifically, not the primary ENI in general.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes inheritance from `eth0`, not an empty set.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes inheritance from `eth0` only, not from every ENI.

citations.title: ENI Creation
citations.quote:
the newly created ENI will
inherit the security group IDs of ``eth0`` of the instance.

questions.stem: A platform team runs a selectorless Service backed by two manually managed EndpointSlice objects. They annotate the first slice with `service.cilium.io/weight: "70"` and the second with `service.cilium.io/weight: "30"`, but the Service uses the default load-balancing algorithm rather than Maglev. What happens to the weights?

options.text: The weights are honoured regardless of algorithm, so traffic splits roughly 70/30.
The weights are only honoured when the Service uses Maglev, so they are not applied.
The weights are rejected and the EndpointSlices are deleted.
The weights are converted into Maglev hash seeds automatically.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that weights are only honoured for the Service referenced by the EndpointSlice when it uses the Maglev load-balancing algorithm, whether configured globally or selected per service. Without Maglev, the weights are not applied.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt explicitly conditions weight honouring on Maglev, so an algorithm-independent split is wrong.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the excerpt says EndpointSlices are deleted for using weights.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt never mentions converting weights into hash seeds.

citations.title: Annotation-based Load Balancing Weight
citations.quote:
Weights are only honored for the Service referenced by that ``EndpointSlice``
when it uses the Maglev load-balancing algorithm, whether Maglev is configured
globally or selected per service through ``service.cilium.io/lb-algorithm``.

questions.stem: After running kubeadm init with the kube-proxy add-on skipped, an engineer joins worker nodes to the cluster. The workers have multiple network interfaces. What must be ensured for Cilium's kube-proxy replacement to work correctly?

options.text: kubelet's --node-ip is set correctly on each worker.
kube-proxy is installed on each worker.
The --cri-socket flag is set on each worker.
The API_SERVER_IP and API_SERVER_PORT are set on each worker.

questions.explanation: The excerpt warns that kubelet's --node-ip must be set correctly on each worker if there are multiple interfaces, otherwise Cilium's kube-proxy replacement may not work correctly. It also suggests validating with kubectl get nodes -o wide to see whether each node has an InternalIP assigned to a device with the same name on each node.

optionRationale.b: kube-proxy is deliberately skipped; installing it would defeat the purpose and is not mentioned as a requirement.
optionRationale.c: The --cri-socket flag is mentioned in the context of kubeadm init, not as a requirement for workers with multiple interfaces.
optionRationale.d: API_SERVER_IP and API_SERVER_PORT are set in the Cilium Helm configuration, not on each worker.

citations.title: Quick-Start

questions.stem: A platform team runs Cilium's eBPF NodePort implementation with the default settings. A client outside the cluster connects to a NodePort service whose backend pod runs on a different node. What does the node receiving the traffic do with the request?

options.text: It redirects the request to the remote backend on its behalf by performing SNAT, and replies from the backend make an extra hop back to that node for reverse translation.
It leaves the packet untouched and the backend replies directly to the external client using the service IP/port as source.
It drops the request because the backend is remote and no tunnel protocol is configured.
It rewrites the destination to the service's externalIP and requires the MTU to be lowered before forwarding.

questions.explanation: In the default SNAT mode, when the node determines the backend is remote, it redirects the request on its behalf by performing SNAT. The trade-off is that backend replies must make the extra hop back to that node for reverse SNAT translation before returning to the client. No MTU change is needed in this mode.

optionRationale.b: This describes DSR mode, which must be enabled explicitly via the loadBalancer.mode Helm option; it is not the default behaviour.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the excerpt says remote backends cause drops; the node forwards them using SNAT.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states SNAT does not require any additional MTU changes, and lowering the MTU is associated with DSR encoding, not SNAT.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR)
citations.quote: the node is redirecting the request to the remote backend on its behalf by performing SNAT. This does not require any additional MTU changes.

questions.stem: An engineer runs `kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg status --verbose | grep XDP` on a node and wants to confirm that kube-proxy XDP acceleration is active. Which output indicates that it has been enabled successfully?

options.text: `XDP Acceleration:    Native`
`XDP Acceleration:    best-effort`
`XDP Acceleration:    hybrid`
`XDP Acceleration:    disabled`

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the acceleration mode can be introspected through the `cilium-dbg status` CLI command and that, if it has been enabled successfully, `Native` is shown. The sample output confirms the line reads `XDP Acceleration:    Native`.

optionRationale.b: `best-effort` is a value of the `loadBalancer.acceleration` setting, not the status output shown for a successfully enabled acceleration.
optionRationale.c: `hybrid` is a value of `loadBalancer.mode`, not the XDP acceleration status value.
optionRationale.d: `disabled` is the default value of the `loadBalancer.acceleration` setting, not the indicator of successful enablement.

citations.title: LoadBalancer & NodePort XDP Acceleration
citations.quote:
If it has been enabled successfully, ``Native``
is shown:

questions.stem: An engineer creates a LoadBalancer service with the annotation service.cilium.io/forwarding-mode: dsr and sets port: 8080 and targetPort: 80. The service is using DSR with IPIP. What is the likely outcome?

options.text: The service will work because IPIP encapsulates the original packet including the port information.
The service will work because the annotation service.cilium.io/forwarding-mode: dsr overrides the port mismatch.
The service will fail because with IPIP the service frontend port must equal the backend target port.
The service will work but only if the backend pods are on nodes labeled service.cilium.io/node=beefy.

questions.explanation: When using the IPIP dispatch, the service frontend port must be equal to the backend (target) port because IPIP does not carry port information. Therefore port 8080 and targetPort 80 will not work. The other options are incorrect: IPIP does not carry port information, the annotation does not override the port requirement, and node labeling is a separate concern for selective exposure.

optionRationale.a: IPIP does not carry port information; the inner packet retains the original destination port, so the backend must listen on the same port.
optionRationale.b: The annotation selects DSR mode but does not change the port matching requirement.
optionRationale.d: Node labeling is relevant for selective service exposure, not for resolving a port mismatch.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR) with IPIP
citations.quote:
When using the IPIP dispatch, the service frontend port must be equal to the
    backend (target) port given IPIP does not carry port information unlike Geneve.

questions.stem: A Service is backed by two EndpointSlice objects with weights 70 and 30. Later, the operator changes the second EndpointSlice from weight 30 to weight 0. What is the effect on traffic?

options.text: The weight 0 is treated as invalid and ignored, so traffic continues at roughly 70/30.
The second slice's backends are removed immediately and all existing connections to them are terminated.
The second slice's backends enter maintenance: existing connections can continue, but new traffic goes entirely to the first slice's backends.
New traffic is split evenly between the two slices because a zero weight resets the distribution.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that a weight of 0 marks those backends as being in maintenance so that existing connections can continue while new traffic is steered to other backends. When the second slice is changed to 0, the first slice receives 100% of the new traffic share.

optionRationale.a: Zero is a valid value; the excerpt says valid values range from 0 to 65535, and invalid values are ignored, but 0 is not invalid.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt says existing connections can continue to use the maintenance backends, so they are not terminated.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states the first slice now receives 100% of the new traffic share, not an even split.

citations.title: Annotation-based Load Balancing Weight
citations.quote:
A weight of ``0`` marks those
backends as being in maintenance so that existing connections can continue
while new traffic is steered to other backends.

questions.stem: A platform team creates a LoadBalancer service with spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges set to 192.168.1.0/24. A pod in the same cluster then connects to the service's ClusterIP. What does Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement do with the source-range field for that connection?

options.text: It ignores the field, so the pod can access the service internally.
It drops the connection because the pod's IP is not in 192.168.1.0/24.
It applies the field only if the pod's IP falls outside the cluster CIDR.
It rewrites the source ranges to the pod CIDR before evaluating the connection.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that when the service is accessed from inside the cluster, the kube-proxy replacement ignores the field whether or not it is set, so any pod or host process in the cluster can reach the LoadBalancer service internally.

optionRationale.b: The field is ignored for in-cluster access, so it cannot cause a drop for a pod connection.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt makes no distinction based on whether the pod IP is inside or outside the cluster CIDR; the field is simply ignored for internal access.
optionRationale.d: No rewriting of source ranges is described; the field is ignored for internal access.

citations.title: LoadBalancer Source Ranges Checks
citations.quote:
When accessing the service from inside a cluster, the kube-proxy replacement will
ignore the field regardless whether it is set.

questions.stem: Which Helm values are required to opt into DSR IPIP on a per-service basis through the service.cilium.io/forwarding-mode: dsr annotation while keeping the global default forwarding mode as SNAT?

options.text: bpf.lbModeAnnotation=true and loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip
loadBalancer.mode=dsr and loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=geneve

questions.stem: A Pod manifest specifies both hostPort and a hostIP of 0.0.0.0. How is the Pod exposed?

optionRationale.b: Loopback is included in the no-hostIP behaviour, but it is not the only exposure.

optionRationale.b: Incorrect because the nodes in Node Group 1 are cordoned and drained, so pods cannot remain on them.
optionRationale.c: Incorrect because the pods are rescheduled, not deleted and manually recreated.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how Cilium treats the numeric values supplied through the service.cilium.io/weight annotation?

options.text: Weights are absolute shares and must total exactly 100 across all slices of a Service.
Weights are relative, may range from 0 to 65535, and invalid values are ignored.
Weights are percentages capped at 100, and any value above 100 is clamped to 100.
Weights are relative but must be positive integers, so 0 is rejected as invalid.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that valid values range from 0 to 65535, that invalid values are ignored, and that weights are relative and do not need to add up to 100.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt explicitly says weights are relative and do not need to add up to 100.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt gives the valid range as 0 to 65535, not a percentage capped at 100.
optionRationale.d: Zero is a valid value that marks backends as being in maintenance, so it is not rejected.

Valid values range from ``0`` to ``65535``. A weight of ``0`` marks those
backends as being in maintenance so that existing connections can continue
while new traffic is steered to other backends. Invalid values are ignored.
Weights are relative and do not need to add up to ``100``.

questions.stem: A new ENI is being created for an instance whose existing ENIs occupy interface indexes 1, 2 and 4, and `spec.eni.first-interface-index` is set to 1. Which interface index is chosen?

5, because it is the next index after the highest one in use.
2, because it is the lowest index currently in use and will be reused.

optionRationale.c: The rule takes the first unused index above the configured value, not the one after the highest index in use.
optionRationale.d: Indexes in use are not reused; the scan looks for an unused one.

questions.stem: A security team wants to block traffic from a specific set of CIDRs while allowing all other traffic to a LoadBalancer service. How can this be achieved with Cilium?

Set service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy: allow and list the CIDRs in loadBalancerSourceRanges.
Set service.cilium.io/type: LoadBalancer and leave loadBalancerSourceRanges empty.
Enable bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true and list the CIDRs in loadBalancerSourceRanges.

optionRationale.c: The type annotation avoids creating corresponding NodePort and ClusterIP services; it does not invert the CIDR list.

questions.stem: What happens on the node hosting the selected backend Pod when a packet arrives encapsulated by DSR with IPIP?

options.text: Cilium forwards the encapsulated packet back to the load balancing node for DNAT.
Cilium terminates the tunnel, strips the outer header, DNATs and delivers the inner packet to the backend Pod identified by the outer destination address.
Cilium drops the packet because IPIP termination must be enabled separately with an additional setting.
Cilium replaces the inner packet's destination with the load balancing node address before delivery.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the encapsulated packet is routed to the node hosting the Pod, where Cilium terminates the tunnel, strips the outer header, DNATs and delivers the inner packet to the backend Pod identified by the outer destination address. It also notes that selecting loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip automatically enables inbound IPIP termination on the backend nodes, so no additional setting is required.

optionRationale.a: The packet is delivered locally after DNAT; it is not sent back to the load balancing node.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says selecting loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip automatically enables the inbound IPIP termination, so no additional setting is required.
optionRationale.d: The inner packet is delivered to the backend Pod identified by the outer destination address; the destination is not replaced with the load balancing node address.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR) with IPIP

The encapsulated packet is routed to the node hosting that Pod, where Cilium
terminates the tunnel, strips the outer header, DNATs and delivers the inner
packet to the backend Pod identified by the outer destination address.

questions.stem: A Service is backed by two EndpointSlices with weights `70` and `30`. Later, the second EndpointSlice is changed from weight `30` to weight `0`. What is the effect on traffic?

The weight `0` is treated as invalid and ignored, so the split stays 70/30.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says existing connections can continue, not that they are reset.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says invalid values are ignored, but `0` is a valid value with a defined maintenance meaning.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states new traffic is steered entirely to the remaining non-maintenance backends.

Run `kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=cilium` and check that every Cilium Pod reports `READY 1/1`.

optionRationale.c: No such command appears in the material; the documented way to verify the feature is the `BandwidthManager` info line from `cilium status`.

questions.stem: A cluster administrator wants to change the kvstore endpoint and credentials that the cilium-agent on every node uses. Which Kubernetes resource in a standard Cilium deployment holds these common configuration values?

options.text: The ConfigMap
The DaemonSet
The Secret
The ClusterRole

questions.explanation: The ConfigMap describes common configuration values passed to the cilium-agent, and the excerpt gives the kvstore endpoint and credentials as an example of such values. The DaemonSet describes the Cilium pod and the agent's command-line options, the Secret holds the credentials used to access the etcd kvstore, and the ClusterRole carries permissions for the Kubernetes API server.

optionRationale.b: The DaemonSet describes the Cilium pod deployed to each node, including the image tag and the command-line options passed to the cilium-agent, not the common configuration values.
optionRationale.c: The Secret describes the credentials used to access the etcd kvstore, but the common configuration values such as the kvstore endpoint are described by the ConfigMap.
optionRationale.d: The ClusterRole is part of the identity and permissions used by cilium-agent to access the Kubernetes API server when RBAC is enabled.

citations.title: Deployment
citations.quote:
A ``ConfigMap`` resource:  describes common configuration values that are
  passed to the cilium-agent, such as the kvstore endpoint and credentials,
  enabling/disabling debug mode, etc.

questions.stem: An operator needs to know which host devices Cilium will treat as native devices for bandwidth enforcement, and wants to override the selection manually. Which description matches the documented behaviour?

options.text: Native devices are auto detected as those with the default route on the host or with Kubernetes InternalIP or ExternalIP assigned, with InternalIP preferred; names can be set manually in the devices helm option, and each listed device must be named the same on all Cilium-managed nodes.
Native devices are auto detected as those carrying the kubernetes.io/egress-bandwidth annotation, and the devices helm option accepts only a single device name.
Native devices are auto detected as those with the default route only; ExternalIP is always preferred over InternalIP when both exist.
Native devices must always be listed manually in the devices helm option, because no auto detection is performed.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says native devices are auto detected as those having the default route on the host or having Kubernetes InternalIP or ExternalIP assigned, with InternalIP preferred over ExternalIP if both exist. Devices can be specified manually in the devices helm option, and each listed device has to be named the same on all Cilium-managed nodes.

optionRationale.b: Annotations are applied to Pods, not used to detect host devices, and the example devices='eth0,eth1,eth2' shows multiple devices are accepted.
optionRationale.c: Auto detection also covers InternalIP or ExternalIP, and InternalIP is preferred over ExternalIP, not the reverse.
optionRationale.d: Auto detection is performed; manual specification is offered as a way to change the detected devices.

citations.title: Bandwidth Manager
citations.quote:
The native host networking devices are auto detected as native devices which have
the default route on the host or have Kubernetes ``InternalIP`` or ``ExternalIP`` assigned.
``InternalIP`` is preferred over ``ExternalIP`` if both exist.

questions.stem: A Pod carries the annotations kubernetes.io/egress-bandwidth: "10M" and kubernetes.io/ingress-bandwidth: "20M". How does Cilium's bandwidth manager enforce each of these two limits?

options.text: Egress is enforced on egress at the native host networking devices using EDT, while ingress is enforced using an eBPF-based token bucket implementation.
Both egress and ingress are enforced using EDT at the native host networking devices.
Egress is enforced using an eBPF-based token bucket implementation, while ingress is enforced using EDT.
Both egress and ingress are enforced by the bandwidth CNI plugin using TBF.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the egress-bandwidth is enforced on egress at the native host networking devices using EDT (Earliest Departure Time), while the ingress-bandwidth is enforced using an eBPF-based token bucket implementation.

optionRationale.b: Only egress uses EDT; ingress uses an eBPF-based token bucket.
optionRationale.c: The mechanisms are the other way round: egress uses EDT and ingress uses the token bucket.
optionRationale.d: The bandwidth manager does not make use of the bandwidth CNI plugin, and TBF is the plugin's mechanism, not Cilium's.

citations.title: Bandwidth Manager
citations.quote:
The ``egress-bandwidth`` is enforced on egress at
the native host networking devices using EDT (Earliest Departure Time), while the ``ingress-bandwidth``
is enforced using an eBPF-based token bucket implementation.

questions.stem: An operator wants the operator to attach Security Groups to new ENIs by matching tags rather than by listing IDs. Which field should be set, and what does the operator do with it?

optionRationale.c: `spec.eni.security-groups` holds Security Group IDs, not tag filters.
optionRationale.d: `spec.eni.subnet-tags` narrows subnets and has nothing to do with Security Group selection.

citations.title: ENI Creation

questions.stem: A cluster uses DSR mode. Because a given backend can serve multiple services, the backend must know which service IP/port to use as the source when replying. How does Cilium convey this, and what is the cost?

options.text: It encodes the information into the packet using a dispatch mechanism, at the cost of advertising a lower MTU.
It performs reverse SNAT on the node that received the request, at no cost to the MTU.
It sets bpf.disableExternalIPMitigation to true, at the cost of losing client source IP preservation.
It relies on the cloud provider's source/destination IP address checking to supply the service IP/port.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that Cilium encodes the service IP/port information into the packet using one of the dispatch mechanisms, at the cost of advertising a lower MTU.

optionRationale.b: Reverse SNAT on the receiving node is the SNAT mode behaviour that DSR avoids, and it is not how the service IP/port is conveyed.
optionRationale.c: That flag concerns the ExternalIP mitigation for CVE-2020-8554 and does not encode service information.
optionRationale.d: Cloud address checking must in some environments be disabled for DSR to work; it does not supply the service IP/port.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR)
citations.quote: Cilium encodes this information into the packet (using one of the dispatch mechanisms described below), at the cost of advertising a lower MTU.

questions.stem: On a node, the configured NodePort range overlaps with the ephemeral port range net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range. What does Cilium do by default, and why?

options.text: It appends the NodePort range to net.ipv4.ip_local_reserved_ports, to prevent a NodePort service from hijacking traffic of a host local application whose source port matches the service port.
It shrinks the ephemeral port range so that the two ranges no longer overlap.
It refuses to start the Cilium agent until the overlap is removed manually.
It disables NodePort services on that node until the overlap is resolved.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says that if the NodePort port range overlaps with the ephemeral port range, Cilium will append the NodePort range to the reserved ports, which is needed to prevent a NodePort service from hijacking traffic of a host local application whose source port matches the service port.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes appending to the reserved ports, not modifying the ephemeral port range itself.
optionRationale.c: No such refusal is described; the excerpt describes an automatic modification of the reserved ports.
optionRationale.d: NodePort services are not disabled; the protection is applied through the reserved ports list.

questions.stem: Kubernetes RBAC is enabled in a cluster running a standard Cilium deployment. The cilium-agent must authenticate to and be authorised by the Kubernetes API server. Which set of resources provides the identity and permissions for this?

options.text: ServiceAccount, ClusterRole, and ClusterRoleBindings
The DaemonSet and its ConfigMap
The Secret holding the etcd kvstore credentials
The ConfigMap holding the kvstore endpoint

questions.explanation: The ServiceAccount, ClusterRole, and ClusterRoleBindings resources provide the identity and permissions used by cilium-agent to access the Kubernetes API server when Kubernetes RBAC is enabled. The Secret and ConfigMap relate to the etcd kvstore, and the DaemonSet describes the Cilium pod itself.

optionRationale.b: The DaemonSet describes the Cilium pod and the ConfigMap carries common configuration values; neither provides the RBAC identity and permissions for the API server.
optionRationale.c: The Secret describes the credentials used to access the etcd kvstore, if required, not the identity and permissions for the Kubernetes API server.
optionRationale.d: The ConfigMap describes common configuration values such as the kvstore endpoint, not the identity and permissions used to access the Kubernetes API server.

citations.title: Deployment
citations.quote:
``ServiceAccount``, ``ClusterRole``, and ``ClusterRoleBindings`` resources:
  the identity and permissions used by cilium-agent to access the Kubernetes
  API server when Kubernetes RBAC is enabled.

questions.stem: An engineer assigns a weight annotation to an EndpointSlice that contributes four backend addresses to a Service. How does the configured weight apply?

options.text: It applies to all backends in that EndpointSlice.
It applies only to the first backend listed in the EndpointSlice.
It is divided evenly among the backends in the EndpointSlice.
It applies only to backends that have no other annotations.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the configured weight applies to all backends in a given EndpointSlice, so every address in that slice shares the same weight.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt makes no distinction between the first and subsequent backends; the weight covers all of them.
optionRationale.c: The weight is not divided among backends; it applies to all backends in the slice.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says nothing about other annotations affecting whether the weight applies.

citations.title: Annotation-based Load Balancing Weight
citations.quote: The configured weight applies to all backends in a given ``EndpointSlice``.

options.text: A `pools.allocated` list with the node's CIDR and `pool: default`.
A `podCIDRs` list with the node's CIDR and an empty `pools` map.
A `pools.requested` list with `needed.ipv4-addrs` and `pool: default`.

optionRationale.d: The post-migration output shows only `pools.allocated`, not `podCIDRs`.

questions.stem: A client pod called mediabot sends traffic to the nginx-service ClusterIP. You run `hubble observe --all` and see a flow from `default/mediabot` to `default/nginx-service:80` marked `pre-xlate-fwd TRACED`, immediately followed by a flow to `default/nginx:80` marked `post-xlate-fwd TRANSLATED`. What do these two events represent?

options.text: The datapath events before and after socket load-balancing translation between the service and the selected service endpoint.
A DNS resolution of the service name followed by the resulting connection to the backend pod.
A policy verdict denying the first flow and allowing the second flow after the endpoint is selected.
The reverse direction of an established connection, first traced and then translated back to the client.

questions.explanation: Hubble prints datapath events before and after socket LB translation between the service and the selected service endpoint, which is exactly what the `pre-xlate-fwd` and `post-xlate-fwd` pair shows: the flow to the service address is traced, then the translated flow to the backend pod is shown.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes socket LB translation between service and endpoint, not DNS resolution; no DNS event appears in the output.
optionRationale.c: The events are marked TRACED and TRANSLATED, not as policy verdicts; the excerpt does not describe a denial.
optionRationale.d: The reverse direction is shown by the `pre-xlate-rev` and `post-xlate-rev` events, not by the forward pair described here.

The ServiceAccount

questions.stem: What does selecting loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip automatically enable on backend nodes?

options.text: It enables Geneve encapsulation for service traffic.
It enables inbound IPIP termination on the backend nodes, stripping the outer header and delivering the inner packet to the local backend Pod.
It enables SNAT forwarding mode globally.
It enables the service.cilium.io/lb-algorithm annotation.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that selecting loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip automatically enables the inbound IPIP termination on the backend nodes (stripping the outer header and delivering the inner packet to the local backend Pod), so no additional setting is required. The other options are incorrect: Geneve is a different dispatch mode, SNAT is a different forwarding mode, and the lb-algorithm annotation is enabled by a different setting (bpf.lbAlgorithmAnnotation=true).

optionRationale.a: Geneve is a different dispatch mode, not enabled by dsrDispatch=ipip.
optionRationale.c: SNAT is a different forwarding mode; dsrDispatch=ipip does not enable it globally.
optionRationale.d: The lb-algorithm annotation is enabled by bpf.lbAlgorithmAnnotation=true, not by dsrDispatch=ipip.

It selects the subnet with the most available addresses.
It selects the subnet that was created most recently.
It selects the subnet with the fewest existing ENIs attached.

questions.stem: An engineer wants to inspect the state and status of the Cilium agent on the node they are logged into, and to validate the state of the eBPF maps directly. Which tool is intended for this?

options.text: The `cilium` command line tool, installed remote from the cluster and using `kubeconfig`.
The Cilium Operator, which manages cluster-wide duties.
The debug CLI client (`cilium-dbg`), which interacts with the REST API of the agent on the same node.
The CNI plugin (`cilium-cni`), which is invoked when a pod is scheduled or terminated.

questions.explanation: The debug CLI client is installed along with the Cilium agent, interacts with the REST API of the agent running on the same node, allows inspecting the local agent's state and status, and provides tooling to access the eBPF maps directly.

optionRationale.a: The ``cilium`` tool is a separate CLI for quick-installing, managing and troubleshooting Cilium on Kubernetes clusters, typically installed remote from the cluster.
optionRationale.b: The operator manages cluster-wide duties and is not a local inspection tool.
optionRationale.d: The CNI plugin is invoked by Kubernetes on pod scheduling or termination; it is not the inspection tool.

questions.stem: An administrator sets nodePort.directRoutingDevice=eth+ on a cluster where several devices match that wildcard. How does Cilium choose the direct routing device?

options.text: It sorts the matching devices in increasing alphanumerical order and picks the first one.
It picks the matching device that carries the Kubernetes ExternalIP, preferring it over InternalIP.
It refuses to start until a single explicit device name is supplied.
It uses all matching devices for direct routing between Cilium nodes.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says that if more than one device matches the wildcard option, Cilium sorts them in increasing alphanumerical order and picks the first one. It also notes that only one device can be used for direct routing between Cilium nodes.

optionRationale.b: The InternalIP/ExternalIP preference applies when no single device was detected or specified and when choosing among devices generally; it is not the rule given for resolving a wildcard match.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt explicitly allows the wildcard option for directRoutingDevice, so no explicit single name is required.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states that only one device can be used for direct routing between Cilium nodes.

questions.stem: An engineer sets `ipam: kubernetes` in the Cilium ConfigMap with `enable-ipv4` set to `true`. Which option is enabled automatically as a result?

`k8s-require-ipv6-pod-cidr`
`enable-ipv6`
`ipam: cluster-pool`

optionRationale.b: The IPv6 PodCIDR requirement is enabled automatically only when `enable-ipv6` is `true`, not when `enable-ipv4` is.
optionRationale.c: `enable-ipv6` is a condition that triggers the IPv6 option; it is not itself enabled by Kubernetes IPAM mode.
