questions.stem: Which statement best captures the scope of what the BGP Control Plane makes reachable from outside the cluster?

options.text: Pod networks and/or Services, for environments that support BGP
Only the cluster's DNS service, via BGP route advertisement
All cluster-internal traffic, because it programs the datapath on every node
Only traffic that has already been observed by Hubble Relay

questions.explanation: The BGP Control Plane makes pod networks and/or Services reachable from outside the cluster for environments that support BGP, by advertising routes to connected routers.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt names pod networks and/or Services, not specifically DNS.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says BGP Control Plane does not program the datapath.
optionRationale.d: Hubble Relay is not part of the described scope; the excerpt ties reachability to BGP route advertisement.

from outside the cluster for environments that support BGP.

questions.stem: An engineer wants to advertise the IP addresses of a local interface to BGP peers using the Interface advertisement type. Which condition must the interface satisfy for its IP addresses to be advertised?

options.text: It must be administratively enabled and in operationally up or unknown state.
It must be administratively enabled and in operationally up state only.
It must be a Cilium-owned interface with addresses managed by Cilium.
It must carry at least one address outside the loopback and link-local ranges, regardless of its state.

questions.explanation: The interface must be administratively enabled and in operationally up or unknown state in order to advertise its IP addresses. Cilium does not manage addresses on arbitrary non-Cilium-owned interfaces, so the node administrator configures them, but Cilium ownership is not a precondition for advertisement.

optionRationale.b: The unknown operational state is also acceptable, not only up.
optionRationale.c: Cilium explicitly does not manage IP addresses on arbitrary non-Cilium-owned local interfaces; the administrator configures them.
optionRationale.d: The interface state is a hard requirement; address ranges only exclude certain addresses from being advertised, they do not replace the state condition.

citations.title: Interface IPs
citations.quote: The interface must be administratively enabled and in operationally ``up`` or ``unknown`` state

questions.stem: In the CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy shown in the attachment, the egressGateway block specifies egressIP: 10.168.60.100. What requirement must this address satisfy?

options.text: It must exist as an IP associated with a network interface on the instance.
It must be the first IPv4 address assigned to the interface named in the interface field.
It must be a public address allocated by the cloud provider.
It must be the address of the node selected by the pod selector's nodeSelector.

questions.explanation: The policy comment for egressIP states that the address must exist as an IP associated with a network interface on the instance. The interface field is an alternative way to choose the egress IP, not a requirement on egressIP.

optionRationale.b: The first IPv4 and IPv6 addresses of an interface are used only when the interface field is specified instead of egressIP.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not require the address to be public or cloud-allocated; it only requires it to be associated with a network interface on the instance.
optionRationale.d: The nodeSelector under selectors restricts which nodes the policy applies to; it does not define the egress IP.

attachments.title: The egress gateway policy under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy
metadata:
  name: egress-sample
spec:
  # Specify which pods should be subject to the current policy.
  # Multiple pod selectors can be specified.
  selectors:
  - podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        org: empire
        class: mediabot
        # The following label selects default namespace
        io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: default
    nodeSelector: # optional, if not specified the policy applies to all nodes
      matchLabels:
        node.kubernetes.io/name: node1 # only traffic from this node will be SNATed
  # Specify which destination CIDR(s) this policy applies to.
  # Multiple CIDRs can be specified.
  destinationCIDRs:
  - "0.0.0.0/0"
  - "::/0"

  # Configure the gateway node.
  egressGateway:
    # Specify which node should act as gateway for this policy.
    nodeSelector:
      matchLabels:
        node.kubernetes.io/name: node2

    # Specify the IP address used to SNAT traffic matched by the policy.
    # It must exist as an IP associated with a network interface on the instance.
    egressIP: 10.168.60.100

    # Alternatively it's possible to specify the interface to be used for egress traffic.
    # In this case the first IPv4 and IPv6 addresses assigned to that interface will be used
    # as egress IP.
    # interface: enp0s8

citations.title: Example policy
citations.quote:
# Specify the IP address used to SNAT traffic matched by the policy.
    # It must exist as an IP associated with a network interface on the instance.

questions.stem: An engineer writes a CiliumBGPClusterConfig with a peer entry that specifies only name, peerASN, peerAddress and a peerConfigRef containing just a name. The manifest is rejected by validation. Which explanation is consistent with how peer configuration references are defined?

The group field of peerConfigRef is mandatory and must always be set explicitly
The kind field of peerConfigRef is mandatory and must always be set explicitly
peerConfigRef must contain the peer autonomous system number rather than a resource name

questions.explanation: Group and kind in peerConfigRef are optional and default to cilium.io and CiliumBGPPeerConfig respectively, so leaving them out is valid. The rejection must therefore stem from something else in the manifest.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt states that group is optional and defaults to cilium.io.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that kind is optional and defaults to CiliumBGPPeerConfig.
optionRationale.d: The peer autonomous system number belongs in the peerASN field, not in peerConfigRef.

questions.stem: In the procedure for shutting down a node that participates in BGP sessions, what is the first step recommended to avoid packet loss as much as possible?

options.text: Drain the node to evict all workloads.
Reconfigure the BGP sessions by modifying the node selector label.
Wait for the BGP peer to remove routes.
Shut down the node.

optionRationale.c: Waiting for route removal is the third step.
optionRationale.d: Shutting down the node is the final step.

questions.stem: A node has an interface named lo carrying several addresses, including a loopback address and an IPv6 link-local address. A CiliumBGPAdvertisement selects that interface with advertisementType "Interface". Which addresses are advertised to BGP peers?

options.text: All IP addresses on the interface, each as an exact /32 or /128 route.
Only the loopback and IPv6 link-local addresses, since those are the stable ones.
The interface's addresses excluding those from the loopback, multicast, IPv6 link-local and IPv4-mapped IPv6 ranges, each as an exact /32 or /128 route.
The interface's addresses aggregated into the smallest covering prefix for the interface.

questions.explanation: Interface IPs are advertised as exact routes, and addresses drawn from the loopback, multicast, IPv6 link-local and IPv4-mapped IPv6 ranges are excluded from advertisement. So the remaining addresses go out as /32 or /128 prefixes, never as an aggregate.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt explicitly excludes several address ranges, so not every address on the interface is advertised.
optionRationale.b: It is the reverse: loopback and IPv6 link-local addresses are among those that are not advertised.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states the addresses are advertised as exact routes (/32 or /128 prefixes), not aggregated.

citations.title: Interface IPs
citations.quote:
The interface IPs are advertised as exact routes (``/32`` or ``/128`` prefixes).
IP addresses from the loopback, multicast, IPv6 link-local and IPv4-mapped IPv6 address ranges are not advertised.

questions.stem: A cluster runs the Cilium BGP Control Plane with no aggregation fields configured on its CiliumBGPAdvertisement resources. A Service of type ClusterIP is assigned the address 10.96.14.37. What prefix does the BGP Control Plane advertise for that service VIP?

options.text: 10.96.14.0/24, the subnet containing the VIP
10.96.14.37/32, the exact route for the VIP
10.96.0.0/16, the cluster's service CIDR
Nothing is advertised until an aggregation length is set

questions.explanation: Without any aggregation configuration, the BGP Control Plane advertises exact routes for service VIPs, which for an IPv4 address means a /32 prefix. The aggregation length fields exist precisely to change this default, so 10.96.14.37/32 is what is advertised here.

optionRationale.a: A /24 is what you would get by setting aggregationLengthIPv4 to 24, but no aggregation is configured in this scenario.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt never mentions advertising the whole service CIDR; the default is the exact VIP route.
optionRationale.d: Aggregation is optional; the default behaviour is to advertise exact routes, not to withhold them.

citations.title: Prefix Aggregation
citations.quote:
By default, the Cilium BGP Control Plane advertises exact routes for service
VIPs (/32 or /128 prefixes).

questions.stem: An egress gateway policy omits both the `egressIP` and the `interface` properties. How does Cilium choose the egress interface and egress IPs?

options.text: It selects the network interface with the default route, and uses the first IPv4 and IPv6 addresses on that interface as the egress IPs.
It selects the first interface in lexical order, and uses the first IPv4 and IPv6 addresses on that interface as the egress IPs.
It performs a route lookup per packet in the datapath and uses the source address chosen by the lookup as the egress IP.
It refuses to select an egress IP, so matching traffic is dropped with the reason `No Egress IP configured`.

questions.explanation: Omitting both properties is a supported configuration: Cilium selects the interface carrying the default route as the egress interface and takes the first IPv4 and IPv6 addresses on it as the egress IPs.

optionRationale.b: Lexical ordering applies to selecting among matching gateway nodes, not to selecting a network interface.
optionRationale.c: Per-packet route lookup in the datapath is how the interface is determined when an explicit egressIP is given, not when both properties are omitted.
optionRationale.d: Omitting both properties is a valid third way of configuring the egress IP, so no drop occurs on that ground.

citations.title: Selecting and configuring the gateway node
citations.quote:
By omitting both ``egressIP`` and ``interface`` properties. This selects the
    network interface with the default route as the egress interface, and the
    first IPv4 and IPv6 addresses on this interface as the egress IPs.

questions.stem: An engineer configures a CiliumBGPPeerConfig with an authSecretRef pointing to a secret containing the correct TCP MD5 password, but the Cilium Agent's pod IP address is address-translated so that the BGP peer sees a different address. What is the result?

options.text: The TCP connection will not succeed and the agent logs will show "dial: i/o timeout".
The TCP connection succeeds because the password is correct, but the session is read-only.
The TCP connection succeeds and the agent logs a warning about address translation.
The CiliumBGPPeerConfig is rejected because TCP MD5 passwords cannot be used with address translation.

questions.explanation: TCP MD5 passwords sign the packet header, so they cannot be used when the session is address-translated by Cilium; the Cilium Agent's pod IP address must be the address the BGP peer sees. optionRationale.d: Hubble Relay is not mentioned in the excerpt, and BGP Control Plane is the feature described for advertising routes.

citations.title: Cilium BGP Control Plane
citations.quote:
BGP Control Plane provides a way for Cilium to advertise routes to connected routers by using the

questions.stem: A node is being shut down for maintenance. The node is selected for BGP by the label enable-bgp=true, and BGP Graceful Restart is disabled. After the engineer runs `kubectl label node <node-name> --overwrite enable-bgp=false`, how quickly should the BGP peer withdraw routes towards the node?

options.text: Immediately after the label change.
After the Stale Timer expires.
After the BGP peer sends a Notification message.
After the node is fully shut down.

questions.explanation: With BGP Graceful Restart disabled, the BGP peer should withdraw routes immediately after the node is unselected by the label change. The excerpt states that if you disable the BGP Graceful Restart feature, the BGP peer should withdraw routes immediately after step 2.

optionRationale.b: The Stale Timer is relevant only when Graceful Restart with Notification is supported by the peer.
optionRationale.c: A Notification is sent by the BGP Control Plane when the node is unselected only if the peer does not support Graceful Restart with Notification; with Graceful Restart disabled, withdrawal is immediate.
optionRationale.d: The withdrawal happens before the node is shut down; waiting until after shutdown would risk breaking traffic.

citations.title: Shutting Down a Node
citations.quote:
If you disable the BGP Graceful Restart feature, the BGP peer should withdraw
  routes immediately after step 2.

questions.stem: An engineer is following the recommended steps to shut down a node that runs Cilium and participates in BGP sessions. The node is selected for BGP by the label enable-bgp=true. After draining the node and changing the label to enable-bgp=false, the engineer waits for the BGP peer to remove routes. What is the purpose of waiting before shutting down the node?

options.text: To allow the BGP peer to remove routes towards the node, because during this period the peer may still send traffic to the node.
To allow the node to re-establish BGP sessions with a new label.
To allow the Cilium agent to restart and apply the new label.
To allow ECMP rehashing to complete before the node is shut down.

questions.explanation: The wait is to give the BGP peer time to remove routes towards the node. During this period, the peer may still send traffic to the node, and shutting down prematurely could break ongoing traffic for Services with externalTrafficPolicy=Cluster.

optionRationale.b: The label change shuts down BGP sessions; the goal is not to re-establish them.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not mention restarting the Cilium agent as part of the procedure.
optionRationale.d: ECMP rehashing occurs after route withdrawal and may cause traffic redirection, but the waiting period is specifically for route removal by the peer.

citations.title: Shutting Down a Node
citations.quote:
Wait for a while until the BGP peer removes routes towards the node. During
   this period, the BGP peer may still send traffic to the node.

questions.stem: A Cilium Egress Gateway policy contains an egressGateway block with nodeSelector matchLabels testLabel: testVal, and three nodes in the cluster carry that label with the names node-c, node-a and node-b. Which node acts as the gateway node for the policy?

options.text: node-a, because the first node in lexical ordering based on node name is selected when several nodes match.
node-c, because the most recently created matching node is selected.
All three nodes act as gateway nodes and share the SNAT work.
No node is selected, because more than one node matches the label set.

questions.explanation: When several nodes match the nodeSelector labels, Cilium picks the first node in lexical ordering based on node name, so node-a is chosen.

optionRationale.b: Selection is by lexical ordering of node names, not by creation time.
optionRationale.c: A single gateway node is selected for the policy; the matching set is narrowed to one node.
optionRationale.d: Multiple matches are resolved by lexical ordering rather than causing the policy to fail.

citations.title: Selecting and configuring the gateway node
citations.quote:
In case multiple nodes are a match for the given set of labels, the
    first node in lexical ordering based on their name will be selected.

questions.stem: An engineer is preparing to shut down a node that runs Cilium and participates in BGP sessions. The node is selected for BGP by the label enable-bgp=true. The engineer first runs `kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets`, then runs `kubectl label node <node-name> --overwrite enable-bgp=false`. What is the immediate effect of the label change on the node's BGP sessions?

options.text: All BGP sessions on the node are shut down.
The BGP sessions remain up but routes are withdrawn after the Stale Timer expires.
The BGP sessions are reset and re-established with a new router ID.
Only BGP sessions for Services with externalTrafficPolicy=Cluster are shut down.

questions.explanation: Changing the CiliumBGPClusterConfig node selector label so that the node is no longer selected shuts down all BGP sessions on that node. The excerpt states that reconfiguring the BGP sessions by modifying or removing the node selector label will shut down all BGP sessions on the node.

optionRationale.b: The Stale Timer applies only when Graceful Restart with Notification is supported by the peer; the label change itself shuts down the sessions immediately.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not mention resetting sessions or changing router IDs; it says the sessions are shut down.
optionRationale.d: The label change affects all BGP sessions on the node, not only those related to a particular service traffic policy.

citations.title: Shutting Down a Node

Reconfigure the BGP sessions by modifying or removing the

questions.stem: An engineer is shutting down a node that participates in BGP sessions. The node is selected by the label enable-bgp=true. The engineer drains the node and then changes the label to enable-bgp=false. BGP Graceful Restart is enabled, and the BGP peer supports Graceful Restart with Notification (RFC 8538). When will the peer withdraw routes towards the node?

options.text: After the Stale Timer defined in RFC 8538 expires.
Immediately after the label change.
After the BGP Control Plane sends a BGP Notification to the peer.
After the node is fully shut down.

questions.explanation: When Graceful Restart is enabled and the peer supports Graceful Restart with Notification, the peer will withdraw routes after the Stale Timer (defined in RFC 8538) expires.

optionRationale.b: Immediate withdrawal occurs when Graceful Restart is disabled or when the peer does not support Graceful Restart with Notification.
optionRationale.c: A BGP Notification is sent when the peer does not support Graceful Restart with Notification, leading to immediate withdrawal, not delayed withdrawal.
optionRationale.d: The withdrawal happens before the node is shut down; the node shutdown is the final step after waiting.

citations.title: Shutting Down a Node
citations.quote:
If the BGP peer supports the Graceful Restart with Notification
    (:rfc:`8538`), it will withdraw routes after the Stale Timer (defined in
    the :rfc:`8538#section-4.1`) expires.

questions.stem: You enable graceful restart on a CiliumBGPPeerConfig. During a Cilium Agent restart, the Agent closes the BGP TCP socket and a TCP FIN reaches the peering BGP router. What does the peer do, and what happens to traffic in the datapath?

options.text: The peer changes its BGP state to `Idle` and starts its `RestartTime` timer, while the datapath continues to forward traffic with no disruption.
The peer immediately withdraws all routes received from the Cilium BGP control plane, and the datapath drops traffic until the session is re-established.
The peer keeps the session in `Established` state and continues receiving route updates from the restarting Agent throughout the restart.
The peer changes its BGP state to `Idle` and starts its `RestartTime` timer, but the datapath stops forwarding traffic until the Agent boots.

questions.explanation: On receiving the TCP FIN, the peer changes its BGP state to `Idle` and starts its `RestartTime` timer. In the event of a Cilium Agent restart, the peering BGP router does not withdraw routes received from the Cilium BGP control plane immediately, and the datapath continues to forward traffic during the Agent restart, so there is no traffic disruption.

optionRationale.b: The peer does not withdraw the routes immediately; that is the point of graceful restart, and the datapath keeps forwarding.
optionRationale.c: The peer moves to `Idle` on receiving the TCP FIN rather than staying in `Established`.
optionRationale.d: The state transition and timer are right, but the datapath continues to forward traffic during the restart, so there is no disruption.

citations.title: Graceful Restart
citations.quote:
On receiving this TCP FIN, the peer changes its BGP state to ``Idle`` and
starts its ``RestartTime`` timer.

questions.stem: An engineer proposes enabling the BGP Control Plane so that pods on different nodes in the same cluster can reach each other. What is wrong with this proposal?

BGP Control Plane only advertises Services, never pod networks
BGP Control Plane does not program the datapath, so it should not be used to establish reachability within the cluster
BGP Control Plane requires an external router inside every node before pod traffic can flow

questions.explanation: The BGP Control Plane advertises routes to connected routers but does not program the datapath. It is therefore unsuitable for establishing reachability inside the cluster; its purpose is making pod networks and/or Services reachable from outside.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt states the opposite: because it does not program the datapath, it should not be used for in-cluster reachability.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt says BGP Control Plane makes pod networks and/or Services reachable from outside, so pod networks are in scope.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes advertising routes to connected routers; it does not require a router on every node.

citations.quote:
Because BGP
Control Plane does not program the datapath , do not use it to establish

questions.stem: A platform team wants a single egress policy to cover two separate sets of gateway nodes, one labelled testLabel=testVal1 and another labelled testLabel=testVal2. Which field should they use to declare both sets in the same policy?

options.text: The `egressGateways` list field, with one entry per node selector.
The `egressGateway` field, repeated once per node selector.
The `nodeSelector` field at the top level of the policy, with multiple `matchLabels` entries.
The `egressGatewayNodes` list field, with one entry per node selector.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that multiple gateway nodes can be selected in the same policy and that they are configured using the `egressGateways` list field. Each entry on that list takes the same configuration options as the singular `egressGateway` field, so two node selectors become two list entries.

optionRationale.b: The singular `egressGateway` field is the single-gateway form; the excerpt describes the list field `egressGateways` for selecting multiple gateway nodes in one policy.
optionRationale.c: `nodeSelector` is a per-entry field inside the gateway configuration, not a top-level field that accepts several `matchLabels` blocks.
optionRationale.d: No field named `egressGatewayNodes` appears in the excerpt; the list field is called `egressGateways`.

egressGateways:
  - nodeSelector:

  - nodeSelector:

questions.stem: A cluster is part of a Cluster Mesh and runs a global NodePort service. A client outside the cluster reaches the service through a node's NodePort and is only ever sent to backends in that same cluster. Cilium is not configured to replace kube-proxy. What explains this?

options.text: Global NodePort services load balance across local and remote backends only when Cilium replaces kube-proxy; otherwise only local backends are eligible through the NodePort.
Global services never include remote backends for NodePort access, regardless of how Cilium is configured.
Remote backends are excluded because the service lacks a service annotation marking it as global.
Remote backends are excluded because the client is outside the cluster and therefore has no Cilium identity.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that global NodePort services load balance across both local and remote backends only if Cilium is configured to replace kube-proxy (kubeProxyReplacement=true). Otherwise, only local backends are eligible for load balancing when accessed through the NodePort, which matches the observed behaviour.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes a configuration-dependent limitation, not an absolute one: with kube-proxy replacement, remote backends do become eligible.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt attributes the behaviour to the kube-proxy replacement setting, not to any service annotation.
optionRationale.d: Client identity is not mentioned; the limitation concerns how the NodePort path selects backends.

citations.title: Limitations
citations.quote:
Global NodePort services load balance across both local and remote backends only
  if Cilium is configured to replace kube-proxy (``kubeProxyReplacement=true``).
  Otherwise, only local backends are eligible for
  load balancing when accessed through the NodePort.

questions.stem: Which statement best contrasts the effect of a zero cache TTL with that of a non-zero cache TTL on an unreachable remote cluster?

options.text: With `"0s"` caches are never revoked, whereas a duration greater than zero causes cached data to be revoked if the connection is not re-established within that duration.
With `"0s"` caches are revoked immediately, whereas a duration greater than zero delays revocation until the connection is re-established.
With `"0s"` only global-service caches are revoked, whereas a duration greater than zero revokes all cached data.
With `"0s"` caches are revoked after fifteen minutes, whereas a duration greater than zero disables revocation.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that the default `"0s"` disables the feature and means caches are never revoked, while setting `clustermesh.cacheTTL` to a duration greater than zero enables revocation of cached data when a lost connection is not re-established within that duration.

optionRationale.b: ``"0s"`` does not revoke immediately; it disables revocation entirely.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt draws no distinction by service type; ``"0s"`` means caches are never revoked.
optionRationale.d: The roles are reversed: ``"0s"`` disables the feature, and ``"15m"`` is an example of an enabling value.

citations.title: Handling Unreachable Clusters
citations.quote: To enable it, set ``clustermesh.cacheTTL`` to a duration greater than zero (e.g., ``"15m"``).

questions.stem: In cluster 1, the global Service rebel-base has service.cilium.io/global: "true" and service.cilium.io/affinity: "local". A client pod in cluster 1 repeatedly curls rebel-base while healthy local backends exist. What should you observe?

Replies come from local backends only, and remote backends are never used even if every local backend is unavailable or unhealthy.

questions.stem: A platform team runs Cluster Mesh across three clusters, each with PodCIDRs drawn from 10.0.0.0/8, and uses a native-routed datapath. questions.stem: After a period of unreachability during which cached data was revoked, connectivity to a remote cluster is re-established. What does Cilium do with that cluster's services?

options.text: The remote cluster's services are repopulated, and load-balancing to its backends resumes.
The remote cluster's services remain revoked until the cache TTL expires again.
The remote cluster's services are repopulated, but load-balancing to its backends stays disabled.
The remote cluster's services are repopulated only if `clustermesh.cacheTTL` is reset to `"0s"`.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that when connectivity is re-established, the remote cluster's services are repopulated, and load-balancing to its backends resumes.

optionRationale.b: Revocation is tied to the lost connection; re-establishing connectivity repopulates the services.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says load-balancing to its backends resumes, not that it stays disabled.

questions.stem: An operator notices that after a remote cluster in a Cluster Mesh became unreachable, global-service traffic is still being directed at backends in that cluster. No cache TTL has been configured. What explains this behaviour?

options.text: Cilium retains the last-known service information in its cache by default, which can lead to traffic being sent to stale or unreachable backends.
Cilium immediately revokes cached data for any cluster whose connection is lost, so the traffic must be coming from a local backend.
Cilium repopulates the remote cluster's services automatically on connection loss, restoring load-balancing to its backends.
Cilium stops load-balancing to the unreachable cluster's backends as soon as the connection drops, regardless of TTL.

questions.explanation: By default, when a remote cluster becomes unreachable, Cilium retains the last-known service information in its cache, and this can lead to traffic being sent to stale or unreachable backends. Revocation only happens if a cache TTL greater than zero has been configured and the connection is not re-established within that duration.

optionRationale.b: Immediate revocation is not the default; the default ``"0s"`` means caches are never revoked.
optionRationale.c: Repopulation happens when connectivity is re-established, not on connection loss.
optionRationale.d: Stopping load-balancing to the unreachable cluster's backends requires a configured TTL and expiry of that duration.

questions.stem: A platform team has a global service in cluster 1 with `service.cilium.io/affinity` set to `local`. All local backends in cluster 1 are healthy. A client in cluster 1 curls the global service. What does it observe?

optionRationale.c: Replies from cluster 2 only would correspond to the `remote` preference, not `local`.

questions.stem: A platform team wants Cilium to drop traffic destined for addresses that are not valid endpoints, and to do so as early as possible for maximum performance. Which Cilium datapath object should they rely on, and which hook does it use?

options.text: The prefilter object, which runs an XDP program and uses CIDR maps supplied by the Cilium agent to look up and drop or allow packets.
The Service object, which performs a map lookup on destination IP and port using the TC ingress hook.
The endpoint policy object, which maps packets to identities and enforces L3/L4 policy.
The socket operations hook, which runs on TCP events in the root cgroup.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the prefilter object runs an XDP program and provides prefilter rules for best performance, using CIDR maps supplied by the Cilium agent so that a packet is either dropped, for example when the destination is not a valid endpoint, or allowed to be processed by the stack. The other objects either operate at a different hook or serve a different purpose.

optionRationale.b: The Service object does perform a map lookup on destination IP and optionally port, but it forwards matching packets to L3/L4 endpoints and is described as usable with the TC ingress hook, not as the XDP-based object that drops traffic for invalid destinations.
optionRationale.c: The endpoint policy object is described as the primary object responsible for mapping packets to identities and enforcing L3 and L4 policies, not as the XDP prefilter that drops traffic to non-endpoint destinations.
optionRationale.d: The socket operations hook is attached to a cgroup and runs on TCP events to monitor state transitions; it is not the XDP-based prefilter object.

questions.stem: An engineer is choosing between the XDP hook and the traffic control ingress hook for a program that must apply L3/L4 endpoint policy and redirect traffic to endpoints. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two hooks?

options.text: The tc ingress hook runs after the networking stack has done initial processing of the packet and has access to most of the metadata associated with a packet, making it ideal for local node processing such as L3/L4 endpoint policy.
The tc ingress hook runs before the networking stack has done any processing of the packet, which is why it is preferred for dropping malicious traffic at the driver.
The XDP hook runs after the L3 layer of the stack and therefore has access to more packet metadata than the tc ingress hook.
The XDP hook is attached to a cgroup and runs on TCP events, whereas the tc ingress hook is attached to a networking interface.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that tc ingress programs are attached to a networking interface, same as XDP, but run after the networking stack has done initial processing of the packet, before the L3 layer, with access to most of the packet metadata, which makes the hook ideal for local node processing such as applying L3/L4 endpoint policy and redirecting traffic to endpoints.

optionRationale.b: This inverts the ordering: tc ingress runs after initial processing, not before any processing; running at the driver is the XDP position.
optionRationale.c: XDP is the earliest hook in the driver, not a hook that runs after the L3 layer.
optionRationale.d: The cgroup-attached hook that runs on TCP events is the socket operations hook, not XDP.

questions.stem: A pod was launched on a node before Cilium was installed, so Cilium does not manage it. Which special identity is assigned to this endpoint?

options.text: reserved:unknown
reserved:unmanaged
reserved:init
reserved:world

questions.explanation: An endpoint that is not managed by Cilium — for example a Kubernetes pod launched before Cilium was installed — is represented by the reserved:unmanaged identity.

optionRationale.a: reserved:unknown is used when the identity could not be derived at all, not for endpoints that Cilium simply does not manage.
optionRationale.c: reserved:init covers an endpoint whose identity has not yet been resolved during bootstrapping, not one that is permanently outside Cilium's management.
optionRationale.d: reserved:world covers any network endpoint outside the cluster, which is broader than an unmanaged in-cluster pod.

attachments.title: Special reserved identities
attachments.body:
+-----------------------------+------------+---------------------------------------------------+
 Identity                     Numeric ID  Description                                       
+=============================+============+===================================================+
 ``reserved:unknown``         0           The identity could not be derived.                
+-----------------------------+------------+---------------------------------------------------+
 ``reserved:host``            1           The local host. Any traffic that originates from  
                                          or is designated to one of the local host IPs.    
+-----------------------------+------------+---------------------------------------------------+
 ``reserved:world``           2           Any network endpoint outside of the cluster       
+-----------------------------+------------+---------------------------------------------------+
 ``reserved:unmanaged``       3           An endpoint that is not managed by Cilium, e.g.   
                                          a Kubernetes pod that was launched before Cilium  
                                          was installed.                                    
+-----------------------------+------------+---------------------------------------------------+
 ``reserved:health``          4           This is health checking traffic generated by      
                                          Cilium agents.                                    
+-----------------------------+------------+---------------------------------------------------+
 ``reserved:init``            5           An endpoint for which the identity has not yet    
                                          been resolved is assigned the init identity.      
                                          This represents the phase of an endpoint in which 
                                          some of the metadata required to derive the       
                                          security identity is still missing. This is       
                                          typically the case in the bootstrapping phase.    
                                                                                            
                                          The init identity is only allocated if the labels 
                                          of the endpoint are not known at creation time.   
+-----------------------------+------------+---------------------------------------------------+
 ``reserved:remote-node``     6           The collection of all remote cluster hosts.       
                                          Any traffic that originates from or is designated 
                                          to one of the IPs of any host in any connected    
                                          cluster other than the local node.                
+-----------------------------+------------+---------------------------------------------------+
 ``reserved:kube-apiserver``  7           Remote node(s) which have backend(s) serving the  
                                          kube-apiserver running.                           
+-----------------------------+------------+---------------------------------------------------+
 ``reserved:ingress``         8           Given to the IPs used as the source address for   
                                          connections from Ingress proxies.                 
+-----------------------------+------------+---------------------------------------------------+

attachments.title: Cross-cluster policy allowing any namespace
attachments.body:
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "allow-cross-cluster-any-ns"
spec:
  description: "Allow x-wing in cluster1 to contact rebel-base in cluster2 (in any NS)"
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      name: x-wing
      io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster: cluster1
  egress:
  - toEndpoints:
    - matchExpressions:
      - key: "k8s:io.kubernetes.pod.namespace"
        operator: "Exists"
      - key: "k8s:io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster"
        operator: "In"
        values:
        - "cluster2"
      - key: "k8s:name"
        operator: "In"
        values:
        - "rebel-base"

The first is to ensure the endpoint is not allowed to send unencrypted traffic to arbitrary targets outside the cluster, achieved by an egress policy that either completely disallows traffic to reserved:world identities or only allows egress to addresses outside the cluster for a subset of trusted IP addresses using toCIDR, toCIDRSet and toFQDN rules.

optionRationale.b: The workaround is framed as an egress policy restricting where pods may send traffic, not an ingress policy on reserved:world.
optionRationale.c: Strict mode ingress concerns cluster-internal ingress traffic arriving other than through the WireGuard tunnel; it is not the egress workaround described.
optionRationale.d: allowRemoteNodeIdentities is a fallback that permits unencrypted traffic associated with a node identity; it does not prevent unencrypted egress.

citations.quote:
This can
be achieved by defining an egress policy which either completely disallows
traffic to ``reserved:world`` identities, or only allows egress traffic
to addresses outside of the cluster to a certain subset of trusted IP
addresses using ``toCIDR``, ``toCIDRSet`` and ``toFQDN`` rules.

questions.stem: Two policy rules partially overlap, so some traffic matches rule one, some matches rule two, and some matches both. Which traffic is allowed?

options.text: Only traffic matching both rules simultaneously.
Only traffic matching exactly one of the two rules.
Traffic matching the union of the two rules.
No traffic, until the overlap is resolved.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that if there is an intersection between two or more rules, traffic matching the union of those rules will be allowed.

optionRationale.a: That describes the intersection, but the excerpt says the union is allowed.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not restrict allowance to traffic matching exactly one rule.
optionRationale.d: There is no requirement to resolve overlap; the union is simply allowed.

citations.title: Rule Basics
citations.quote:
If there is an intersection between two or more rules,
then traffic matching the union of those rules will be allowed.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes endpointSelector / nodeSelector in Cilium?

options.text: Host is an extended POSIX regex matched against the host header of a request, e.g. ``foo.com``. If omitted or empty, the value of the host header is ignored.

With never mode, policy enforcement is disabled on all endpoints, even if rules do select specific endpoints. In other words, all traffic is allowed from any source (on ingress) or destination (on egress).

questions.explanation: Selects the endpoints or nodes which the policy rules apply to. The policy rules will be applied to all endpoints which match the labels specified in the selector. For additional details, see the EndpointSelector and NodeSelector sections.

optionRationale.c: This describes ingress, not endpointSelector / nodeSelector.

questions.stem: A team wants to allow traffic to a set of pods from 10.0.0.0/8, but must exclude the subnet 10.1.0.0/16 from that range. Which policy field supports this exclusion?

options.text: fromCIDR
fromCIDRSet
endpointSelector
fromCIDRGroup

questions.explanation: `fromCIDRSet` allows a list of source prefixes/CIDRs together with an optional list of subnets of those prefixes from which communication is not allowed, so it is the field that can express the exclusion. `fromCIDR` only lists allowed prefixes and has no exclusion mechanism.

optionRationale.a: `fromCIDR` lists source prefixes that are allowed, but offers no way to carve out a disallowed subnet.
optionRationale.c: `endpointSelector` selects the destination endpoints the rule applies to, not the source CIDRs.
optionRationale.d: `fromCIDRGroup` is not a field; CIDR groups are referenced indirectly through `fromCIDRSet`.

citations.title: Ingress
citations.quote:
List of source prefixes/CIDRs that are allowed to talk to all endpoints

questions.stem: How does Cilium handle the start of additional pods labelled role=frontend once the first such pod has already been given an identity that is permitted to initiate connections to the identity of the role=backend pod?

options.text: It resolves the identity via a key-value store, with no action performed on any cluster node hosting role=backend pods.
It installs a new IP address filter on every node hosting a role=backend pod before the pod is allowed to start.
It assigns a fresh, unique identity to each new pod, which must then be separately allowed to reach the role=backend identity.
It delays the new pod until every cluster node has been updated with the security rules for that pod.

questions.explanation: Because Cilium bases security on a label-derived identity that can be shared between pods, starting further role=frontend pods only requires resolving that identity via a key-value store; nothing has to be done on the nodes hosting role=backend pods, and the start is delayed only until the identity is resolved.

optionRationale.b: Installing IP address filters on backend nodes is the traditional approach that Cilium replaces, not what Cilium does.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states the identity can be shared between pods, so subsequent frontend pods reuse the existing identity rather than each needing a new one.
optionRationale.d: Updating security rules on all other cluster nodes is the costly step Cilium avoids; only identity resolution is required.

citations.title: Identity-Based
citations.quote:
The subsequent start of additional ``role=frontend`` pods
only requires to resolve this identity via a key-value store, no action has to
be performed on any of the cluster nodes hosting ``role=backend`` pods.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes IPs in Cilium?

Obtained via intercepting DNS requests with a proxy.

questions.stem: Which entity should be used in a CiliumNetworkPolicy to allow traffic from the Cilium Envoy instance that handles ingress L7 traffic, including pod-to-pod traffic within the same cluster when using ingress endpoints?

`host`
`remote-node`
`health`

optionRationale.b: `host` includes the local host and containers running in host networking mode, not the Envoy ingress instance.
optionRationale.c: `remote-node` covers any node in connected clusters other than the local host, not the ingress proxy.
optionRationale.d: `health` represents health endpoints used to check cluster connectivity health, not ingress L7 traffic.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that policy rules imported via Kubernetes automatically get the label `io.cilium.k8s.policy.name=NAME` assigned, where `NAME` corresponds to the name specified in the resource.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt gives the label key as `io.cilium.k8s.policy.name`, not a namespace key.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt gives the label key as `io.cilium.k8s.policy.name`, not a description key.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the label is assigned automatically on import.

questions.stem: You are validating WireGuard encryption on a three-node cluster. You open a bash shell in a Cilium pod and run `cilium-dbg status | grep Encryption`. Which output indicates that WireGuard has been enabled correctly?

options.text: `Encryption: Wireguard [cilium_wg0 (Pubkey: <..>, Port: 51871, Peers: 2)]`
`Encryption: Wireguard [cilium_wg0 (Pubkey: <..>, Port: 51871, Peers: 3)]`
`Encryption: Wireguard [cilium_wg0 (Pubkey: <..>, Port: 51871, Peers: 0)]`
`Encryption: Disabled`

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the number of peers should correspond to the number of nodes subtracted by one. On a three-node cluster that is two peers, which matches the sample output showing `Peers: 2`.

optionRationale.b: This equals the full node count rather than the node count minus one, so it does not match the stated expectation.
optionRationale.c: Zero peers would not correspond to a number of nodes subtracted by one on a three-node cluster.
optionRationale.d: This reports encryption as disabled, which contradicts the goal of confirming WireGuard is enabled.

citations.title: Validate the Setup
citations.quote:
Check that WireGuard has been enabled (number of peers should correspond to
   a number of nodes subtracted by one)

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between fromRequires and fromEndpoints in a CiliumNetworkPolicy?

options.text: fromRequires sets additional constraints that must be met for the selected endpoints to be reachable, but does not grant access by itself; fromEndpoints rules are also needed to allow traffic.
fromRequires grants access to all endpoints that meet its constraints, making fromEndpoints unnecessary.
fromEndpoints sets base requirements, and fromRequires allows specific traffic.
fromRequires and fromEndpoints are mutually exclusive and cannot be used together.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that fromRequires is a list of additional constraints which must be met for the selected endpoints to be reachable. These constraints do not grant access privileges by themselves, so to allow traffic there must also be rules which match fromEndpoints.

optionRationale.b: fromRequires does not grant access; it only sets requirements.
optionRationale.c: The roles are reversed: fromRequires sets base requirements, fromEndpoints allows traffic.
optionRationale.d: They are designed to be used together, as the excerpt shows.

citations.title: Additional Label Requirements
citations.quote:
``fromRequires`` is a list of additional constraints which must
be met in order for the selected endpoints to be reachable. These additional
constraints do not grant access privileges by themselves, so to allow traffic
there must also be rules which match ``fromEndpoints``.

questions.stem: An engineer wants Cilium to permit all traffic from any source on ingress and to any destination on egress, regardless of which CiliumNetworkPolicies select the endpoints. Which policy enforcement mode achieves this?

options.text: default
always
never
audit

questions.explanation: `never` mode disables policy enforcement on all endpoints, even if rules do select specific endpoints, so all traffic is allowed from any source on ingress or to any destination on egress.

optionRationale.a: In `default` mode, an endpoint that is selected by a policy permits only allowed traffic, so selecting policies would still restrict it.
optionRationale.b: `always` mode does the opposite: it enforces policy on all endpoints even when no rules select them.
optionRationale.d: `audit` is not one of the three policy enforcement modes described.

citations.title: Policy Enforcement Modes
citations.quote:
With never mode, policy enforcement is disabled on all endpoints, even if
  rules do select specific endpoints. In other words, all traffic is allowed
  from any source (on ingress) or destination (on egress).

questions.stem: A Cilium cluster uses transparent encryption. An endpoint is permitted to initiate traffic to targets outside the cluster. A new pod is created on a remote node, but the local node has not yet learned that the pod's IP address belongs to a Cilium-managed endpoint. During this time, the endpoint sends packets to that IP address. What does Cilium do with those initial packets?

options.text: It sends them unencrypted, because it must assume the destination IP address is outside the cluster.
It drops them until the endpoint information has propagated.
It encrypts them using the local node's encryption key.
It encrypts them using the encryption key of the remote node.

questions.explanation: Transparent encryption uses the same mechanisms as policy enforcement to decide whether a destination belongs to a Cilium-managed endpoint on a remote node. Until Cilium learns that a particular IP address belongs to a remote Cilium-managed endpoint or newly joined remote Cilium host, it has to assume the destination is outside the cluster, so the initial packets are sent unencrypted. Only once the information has propagated and Cilium knows the IP address is an endpoint on a remote node does it start encrypting packets using the encryption key of the remote node.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the initial packets are sent out unencrypted, not dropped; dropping would be a policy action, not the described encryption behaviour.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that once the endpoint is known, encryption uses the encryption key of the remote node, not the local node's key.
optionRationale.d: Encryption with the remote node's key begins only after Cilium knows the IP address is an endpoint on a remote node; before that, packets are unencrypted.

citations.title: Egress traffic to not yet discovered remote endpoints may be unencrypted
citations.quote:
In such a case there is a time window during which Cilium will send out the
initial packets unencrypted, as it has to assume the destination IP address is
outside of the cluster.

questions.stem: An engineer is examining the realised policy for endpoint 568 and wants to list the labels of each ingress rule that applies to it. Which command should they use?

`cilium-dbg endpoint list`

`cilium-dbg endpoint get 568 -o jsonpath='{range ..status.policy.realized.l4.egress[*].derived-from-rules}{@}{"\n"}{end}'`

questions.explanation: The excerpt provides this exact command to print out the ingress labels for endpoint 568.

optionRationale.b: `cilium-dbg endpoint list` provides endpoint data but not the labels of each ingress rule.
optionRationale.c: `cilium-dbg policy get` without labels returns the complete policy, not the per-rule labels for an endpoint.
optionRationale.d: This command targets egress rules, not ingress rules.

citations.quote: cilium-dbg endpoint get 568 -o jsonpath='{range ..status.policy.realized.l4.ingress[*].derived-from-rules}{@}{"\n"}{end}'

questions.stem: A policy author writes a `toPorts` entry that specifies a port and protocol but leaves both the `http` and `dns` fields unset. How is traffic to that port treated at layer 7?

options.text: All traffic is denied until a layer 7 rule is added.
No additional port level rules are applied, so all traffic is permitted.
The policy is rejected because a union member must always be set.
Traffic is permitted only for HTTP, as the default protocol.

questions.explanation: The `L7Rules` comment states that if none of the union members are specified, no additional port level rules are applied, and the excerpt adds that if no rules are specified then all traffic is permitted.

optionRationale.a: An empty rule set permits rather than denies; the excerpt says all traffic is permitted.
optionRationale.c: The fields are marked optional and the excerpt explicitly covers the case where none are specified.
optionRationale.d: No default protocol is described; with no rules, all traffic is permitted.

citations.quote: If none are specified, then no additional port level rules are applied.

questions.stem: After enabling encryption, a Cilium Pod starts but its logs contain a warning similar to `Device eth0 does not exist`. How should this be addressed?

options.text: Set the encryption interface with `--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX`
Increase the delay before old key cleanup with the agent flag `ipsec-key-rotation-duration`
Perform a new key rotation, properly, so that the SPI is incremented
Move the IPsec Secret into the same namespace as Cilium

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that if there is a warning message similar to `Device eth0 does not exist`, the remedy is to use `--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX` to set the encryption interface. The other options address different problems: key rotation timing, SPI mismatches and Secret placement.

optionRationale.b: The ipsec-key-rotation-duration flag controls how long before old keys are cleaned up after a rotation; it has nothing to do with a missing device warning.
optionRationale.c: A proper new key rotation is the fix given for XfrmInStateProtoError caused by a key update without incrementing the SPI, not for a missing interface warning.
optionRationale.d: Namespace co-location of the Secret and Cilium is the check for Pods that fail to start, not for a device warning in a running Pod's logs.

citations.title: Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
If there is a warning message similar to ``Device eth0 does not exist``,
     use ``--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX`` to set the encryption
     interface.

questions.stem: A deny policy is deployed that denies ingress from "world" on all namespaces on all Pods managed by Cilium. What happens to existing inter-cluster policies?

options.text: They are also blocked, because the deny policy covers all namespaces.
They are still allowed, because the policy allows traffic from everywhere except from "world".
They are blocked only if they are Kubernetes Network Policies rather than Cilium policies.
They are unaffected only if they were created before the deny policy.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that existing inter-cluster policies will still be allowed, as the policy is allowing traffic from everywhere except from "world".

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says the opposite: inter-cluster policies remain allowed.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not distinguish policy kinds for this outcome.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt gives no role to creation order for this outcome.

citations.title: Deny Policies
citations.quote:
Existing inter-cluster policies will still be allowed
as this policy is allowing traffic from everywhere except from "world".

questions.stem: A policy uses matchPattern: *.cilium.io. Which set of queries does this pattern allow?

options.text: cilium.io and all of its subdomains, including cilium.io itself.
Only cilium.io, because the leading wildcard is ignored for the apex domain.
sub.cilium.io but not cilium.io, because the wildcard does not match the dot separator.
Any name containing the string cilium.io anywhere, such as notcilium.io.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that a wildcard within a domain allows 0 or more valid DNS characters except the dot separator, so *.cilium.io matches sub.cilium.io but not cilium.io. The apex domain is therefore excluded.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt explicitly says *.cilium.io will not match cilium.io.
optionRationale.b: The wildcard is not ignored; it matches characters other than the dot separator, so subdomains match while the apex does not.
optionRationale.d: The pattern is anchored to the literal cilium.io domain; the excerpt gives no support for matching arbitrary names containing that string.

citations.title: DNS Policy and IP Discovery
citations.quote:
``*`` within a domain allows 0 or more valid DNS characters, except for the
    ``.`` separator. ``*.cilium.io`` will match ``sub.cilium.io`` but not
    ``cilium.io``.

questions.stem: After enabling encryption, the Cilium Pods fail to start. What should be checked first?

options.text: Whether the IPsec Secret and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together.
Whether the `ipsec-key-rotation-duration` agent flag has been increased.
Whether the decryption interface list includes all native devices.
Whether the `XfrmOutPolBlock` counter is non-zero.

questions.explanation: If the Cilium Pods fail to start after enabling encryption, the guidance is to double-check whether the IPsec Secret and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together.

optionRationale.b: The `ipsec-key-rotation-duration` flag is used to increase the delay before old key cleanup when key rotation is expected to take longer, not to fix Pods that fail to start.
optionRationale.c: The decryption interface list is checked with `cilium-dbg encrypt status` once encryption is running, not as a first step when Pods fail to start.
optionRationale.d: `XfrmOutPolBlock` is an XFRM error counter for packets Cilium dropped that would otherwise have left the node in plain-text; it is not the first thing to check when Pods fail to start.

citations.title: Troubleshooting
citations.quote: If the ``cilium`` Pods fail to start after enabling encryption, double-check if the IPsec ``Secret`` and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together.

questions.stem: A layer 7 HTTP rule list contains three separate rules. An incoming HTTP request matches only the second of them. What is the result?

options.text: The request is denied, because all rules must match.
The request is permitted, because at least one of the rules matches.
The request is permitted only if the first rule also matches.
The request is dropped at the network layer without any application response.

questions.explanation: Each member of `L7Rules` consists of a list of application protocol rules, and a layer 7 request is permitted if at least one of the rules matches.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt states the opposite: matching at least one rule is sufficient.
optionRationale.c: There is no requirement for the first rule to match; any single match suffices.
optionRationale.d: For layer 7 violations the excerpt says an application protocol specific access denied message is crafted where possible, not a silent packet drop.

citations.title: Layer 7 Policies

request is permitted if at least one of the rules matches.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Standalone DNS Proxy in Cilium?

options.text: List of destination prefixes/CIDRs that endpoints selected by ``endpointSelector`` are allowed to talk to, along with an optional list of prefixes/CIDRs per source prefix/CIDR that are subnets of the destination prefix/CIDR to which communication is not allowed.

With never mode, policy enforcement is disabled on all endpoints, even if rules do select specific endpoints. In other words, all traffic is allowed from any source (on ingress) or destination (on egress).
Not encrypted when they are destined to the same node from which they were sent.
Independent component that runs as a separate DaemonSet in the cluster, providing DNS proxying capabilities independent of the Cilium agent.

optionRationale.c: This describes Packets, not Standalone DNS Proxy.
optionRationale.a: This describes toCIDRSet, not Standalone DNS Proxy.
optionRationale.b: This describes never, not Standalone DNS Proxy.

citations.title: Standalone DNS Proxy (alpha)
